\]

Therefore we must have \(c=1\).
Thus the only possible value is \(c=1\), so \(\boxed{1}\).

Using \(x=\cos\theta,\; y=\sin\theta\), we get \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{3\cos\theta-4\sin\theta}{4\cos\theta+3\sin\theta}=\dfrac{3-4\tan\theta}{4+3\tan\theta}\), so \(\tan\theta(4+3\tan\theta)=3-4\tan\theta\).

\]

Since minimizing \(d(n)\) is equivalent to minimizing \(3^{-k}\), we want the largest possible exponent \(k\) such that \(n=3^k n'\) with \(3\nmid n'\) and \(1\le n<100\).
The smallest possible distance occurs when \(k\) is maximal, so we need the largest \(k\) such that some \(n<100\) is divisible by \(3^k\) (i.e., \(n\) contains \(3^k\) as a factor); since \(3^4=81<100\) but \(3^5=243>100\), the maximal \(k\) is \(4\).
Since \(k=4\), the closest houses must be the positive integers \(n<100\) with \(3^4\mid n\) but \(3^5\nmid n\), i.e. \(n=81\cdot t\) where \(t\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) and \(3\nmid t\); because \(n<100\), we have \(81t<100\), so \(t=1\) only, giving the unique closest house \(n=81\).
Thus \(d(n)=3^{-k}\) is minimized by \(n=81\), and \(d(81)=3^{-4}=\boxed{\tfrac1{81}}\).

Choose any 3 sides of the regular 16-gon (to extend) and note that two choices are congruent exactly when the pattern of their starting vertices around the 16-gon differs by rotation, so count distinct triples of side positions up to rotation.
Fix a starting vertex for the first extended side to break rotational symmetry; then the other two extended sides correspond to choosing two further starting positions among the remaining \(15\), with the condition that the resulting three lines form a triangle whose vertices do not lie on the original 16-gon—this fails exactly when one chosen pair are opposite (i.e., the extended sides are separated by \(8\) edges), so the number of valid noncongruent triples is
\[
\frac{1}{16}\left(\binom{16}{3}-16\binom{1}{1}\binom{14}{1}\right)=\frac{1}{16}\left(560-112\right)=28.
\]
\[
\text{Thus the number of noncongruent triangles is } \boxed{28}.
\]

At the stopping time, the process ends exactly when the second occurrence of either color appears, so the table contains either **RR** (and no other color has repeated yet) or **GG** (and no other color has repeated yet); therefore the desired probability is
\[
\mathbb P(\text{at least one red and one green at stop})
= \mathbb P(\text{the first repeated-color is red and green has appeared before that})
+ \mathbb P(\text{the first repeated-color is green and red has appeared before that}). 
\]
\[
\mathbb P(\text{first repeat is }RR)=\frac{\binom{4}{2}\binom{3}{0}}{\binom{7}{2}}=\frac{6}{21}=\frac{2}{7}\,.
\]
\[
\mathbb P(\text{first repeat is }GG)=\frac{\binom{3}{2}\binom{4}{0}}{\binom{7}{2}}=\frac{3}{21}=\frac{1}{7}\,.
\]
\[
\mathbb P(\text{stop with at least one red and one green})
=1-\mathbb P(\text{stop with }RR)-\mathbb P(\text{stop with }GG)
=1-\frac{2}{7}-\frac{1}{7}=\boxed{\frac{4}{7}}.
\]

\[

Since each move flips exactly \(k\) switches, the total number of “on” switches changes by
\[
\Delta = k-2t
\]
where \(t\) is the number of currently-on switches among the \(k\) flipped ones; thus \(\Delta \equiv k \pmod 2\). Starting from 0 on switches, after \(m\) minutes the number of on switches has parity \(\equiv mk \pmod 2\). To have all \(n\) switches on at the end, we need
\[
mk \equiv n \pmod 2.
\]

Let \(a_i=x_i\) and define \(y_k=x_k-x_{k+n}\) for \(k=1,\dots,n\); then
\[
\sum_{1\le r<s\le 2n}(s-r-n)x_rx_s
=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^n\sum_{l=1}^n (k-l)\,y_k y_l
=\sum_{k=1}^n (2k-n-1)\,y_k\left(\sum_{l=1}^k y_l\right),
\]
so we may maximize by taking each \(y_k\in[-2,2]\) at an endpoint.
Let \(S_k=\sum_{l=1}^k y_l\); then the expression becomes
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n (2k-n-1)\,y_k\,S_k
\]
and we maximize by choosing \(y_k=2\,\mathrm{sgn}(S_k)\in\{\pm2\}\) for each \(k\), so the maximum occurs at the endpoint choice \(y_k\in\{\pm2\}\).
Take \(y_k=2\,\mathrm{sgn}(S_k)\) so that \(S_k=\sum_{l=1}^k y_l=2k\) for all \(k\), hence the maximum value equals
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n (2k-n-1)\,(2)\,(2k)=4\sum_{k=1}^n(2k-n-1)k.
\[
4\sum_{k=1}^n(2k-n-1)k
=4\left(\sum_{k=1}^n(2k^2)-(n+1)\sum_{k=1}^n k\right)
=4\left(2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}-(n+1)\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right).
\]
\[
4\left(2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}-(n+1)\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)
=4(n+1)\left(\frac{n(2n+1)}{3}-\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right).
\]
\[

=4(n+1)\left(\frac{2n(2n+1)-3n(n+1)}{6}\right)
=\frac{4n(n+1)\bigl(4n+2-3n-3\bigr)}{6}
=\frac{2n(n+1)(n-1)}{3}.
\]
The maximum value is therefore \(\boxed{\frac{2n(n+1)(n-1)}{3}}\).

Let \(x=\operatorname{Arcsin}(\sin t)\), \(y=\operatorname{Arccos}(\cos t)=\frac{\pi}{2}-\operatorname{Arcsin}(\cos t)\), and \(z=\operatorname{Arctan}(\tan t)\); then a three-term arithmetic progression implies either \(2y=x+z\) (if \(y\) is the middle term) or \(2x=y+z\) or \(2z=x+y\).
Since \(\operatorname{Arcsin}(\sin t)\in[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}]\), \(\operatorname{Arccos}(\cos t)\in[0,\pi]\), and \(\operatorname{Arctan}(\tan t)\in(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2})\), for the least positive \(t\) we take \(y\) as the middle term, so we impose the arithmetic progression condition
\[
2\,\operatorname{Arccos}(\cos t)=\operatorname{Arcsin}(\sin t)+\operatorname{Arctan}(\tan t).
\]
Let \(t\in(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2})\) (the least positive case), so \(\operatorname{Arcsin}(\sin t)=t\), \(\operatorname{Arccos}(\cos t)=\tfrac{\pi}{2}-t\), and \(\operatorname{Arctan}(\tan t)=t\); then
\[
2\Big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-t\Big)=t+t \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \pi-2t=2t \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; t=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]
Verify the values at \(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\): \(\operatorname{Arcsin}(\sin t)=\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\operatorname{Arccos}(\cos t)=\frac{\pi}{4}\), \(\operatorname{Arctan}(\tan t)=\frac{\pi}{4}\), giving common difference \(0\), so we must look beyond this case.
Since for \(t\in(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2})\) we get \( \operatorname{Arcsin}(\sin t)=t,\ \operatorname{Arccos}(\cos t)=\tfrac{\pi}{2}-t,\ \operatorname{Arctan}(\tan t)=t\), the only possible arithmetic-progression conditions are
\[
2\Big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-t\Big)=t+t \ \Rightarrow\ t=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\quad(\text{leads to difference }0),
\]
or else \(2t=(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-t)+t\) (or \(2t=t+(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-t)\)), which would force \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}=2t\Rightarrow t=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\) again; hence the least positive \(t\) must lie outside \((0,\tfrac{\pi}{2})\).
Consider the next interval \(t\in\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)\), where \(\operatorname{Arcsin}(\sin t)=\pi-t\), \(\operatorname{Arccos}(\cos t)=\pi-t\), and \(\operatorname{Arctan}(\tan t)=t-\pi\); then impose \(2\,\operatorname{Arccos}(\cos t)=\operatorname{Arcsin}(\sin t)+\operatorname{Arctan}(\tan t)\):
For \(t\in\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)\), the arithmetic progression condition becomes
\[
2(\pi-t)=(\pi-t)+(t-\pi)\;,
\]
so
\[
2\pi-2t= -t \;\Longrightarrow\; 2\pi=t\;.
\]
\[
t=2\pi. \boxed{2\pi}
\]

From \((1)\), substitute \(x^2y=-z(y^2+z)\) into the second equation to get
\[
z^3+z^2y+zy^3-z(y^2+z)=\frac14(x^4+y^4).\tag{2}
\]
From (2), factor the left-hand side:
\[
z^3+z^2y+zy^3-z(y^2+z)=z^2y+zy^3=z y(z+y^2),
\]
so
\[
z y(z+y^2)=\frac14(x^4+y^4).\tag{3}
\]
Using (1) to eliminate \(x^4\), note \(x^2y=-z(y^2+z)\Rightarrow x^4=\dfrac{z^2(y^2+z)^2}{y^2}\), so (3) becomes
\[
zy(z+y^2)=\frac14\left(\frac{z^2(y^2+z)^2}{y^2}+y^4\right).
\]
Multiply both sides by \(4y^2\) to clear denominators:
\[
4y^2\cdot zy(z+y^2)=z^2(y^2+z)^2+y^6
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
4zy^3(z+y^2)=z^2(y^2+z)^2+y^6. \tag{4}
\]
Let \(y\neq 0\) and set \(t=\dfrac{z}{y}\). Then \(z=ty\) and (4) becomes
\[
4(ty)y^3(ty+y^2)=(ty)^2(y^2+ty)^2+y^6
\;\Longrightarrow\;
4t^2(t+1)=t^2(1+t)^2+1. \tag{5}
\]
From (5),
\[
4t^2(t+1)=t^2(t+1)^2+1 \;\Longrightarrow\; t^2(t+1)(4-(t+1))=1
\;\Longrightarrow\; t^2(t+1)(3-t)=1. \tag{6}
\]
From \(t^2(t+1)(3-t)=1\), expand to get
\[
t^2( (t+1)(3-t))=t^2( -t^2+2t+3)=1
\;\Longrightarrow\;
t^4-2t^3-3t^2+1=0.
\]
Factor \(t^4-2t^3-3t^2+1\) as
\[
t^4-2t^3-3t^2+1=(t^2+at-1)(t^2+bt-1),
\]
so comparing coefficients gives \(a+b=-2\) and \(ab-2= -3\), hence \(a=1+\sqrt5,\ b=1-\sqrt5\), and therefore
\[
t^4-2t^3-3t^2+1=(t^2+(1+\sqrt5)t-1)(t^2+(1-\sqrt5)t-1).
\]

Take \(a=d\) and \(a=2d\) to get, respectively, that for any \(x,y,z\in X\),
\[
\max\{|x|,\ |y-d|,\ |z-2d|\}>t d
\quad\text{and}\quad
\max\{|x-d|,\ |y-2d|,\ |z-3d|\}>t d,
\]
so in particular no two points of \(X\) can lie within distance \(td\) of the same translate \((a-d)\) as \(d\) varies.
Fix \(d>0\) and take \(a=d\) in the given inequality with \(x=y=z\in X\); then
\[
\max\{|x-(d-d)|,\ |x-d|,\ |x-(d+d)|\}=\max\{|x|,\ |x-d|,\ |x-2d|\}>td,
\]
so for every \(x\in X\) and every \(d>0\),
\[
\max\{|x|,\ |x-d|,\ |x-2d|\}>td. 
\]
Fix \(x\in X\) and choose \(d=|x|/2>0\); then \(\{|x|,|x-d|,|x-2d|\}=\left\{|x|,\left|\frac{x}{2}\right|,\left|0\right|\right\}\), so the inequality gives \(\max\{|x|,\ |x|/2,\ 0\}=|x|>t\cdot (|x|/2)\), hence \(2>t\).
Take \(d>0\) and choose \(a=x+d\) with \(x=y=z\in X\); then
\[
\max\{|x-(a-d)|,\ |x-a|,\ |x-(a+d)|\}
=\max\{0,\ d,\ 2d\}=2d>td,
\]
so \(2>t\).
\[
\text{Since the previous step shows }2>t\text{ for all valid }t,\ \text{it remains to check that any }0<t\le 2\text{ is attainable by constructing such an }X.
\]
Let \(0<t\le2\) and set \(X=\{\,n d_0 : n\in\mathbb Z\,\}\) for some fixed \(d_0>0\); then for any \(a\in\mathbb R,\ d>0\) and \(x,y,z\in X\), the three numbers \(x-(a-d),\,y-a,\,z-(a+d)\) are respectively at least \(d_0^{-1}\) times the pairwise distances between lattice points, so their absolute values cannot all be \(\le td\), forcing \(\max\{|x-(a-d)|,|y-a|,|z-(a+d)|\}>td\) whenever \(t\le2\).
To finish the construction for \(0<t\le 2\), let \(X=d_0\mathbb Z\) and note that among the three points \(x-(a-d),\,y-a,\,z-(a+d)\) at least two differ by a nonzero multiple of \(d_0\), so their distances to \(0\) cannot all be \(\le td\); hence the maximum must exceed \(td\), and therefore the inequality holds for all \(a\in\mathbb R\), \(d>0\), and \(x,y,z\in X\).
Therefore, the set of all positive real numbers is exactly \(\boxed{(0,\,2]}\).

Let the cutting lines form a planar graph whose vertices are intersection points of cut segments; since every polygonal piece has interior angles only \(45^\circ\) or \(90^\circ\), every vertex angle in the induced tiling is a multiple of \(45^\circ\), so the total angle around any interior vertex must be a multiple of \(360^\circ\).
At each interior tiling vertex, the total angle is a multiple of \(360^\circ\) built from \(45^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\), so the number of \(45^\circ\) angles meeting there plus twice the number of \(90^\circ\) angles meeting there must equal \(8\) (i.e., \(45a+90b=360\Rightarrow a+2b=8\)).
Since \(a+2b=8\) with \(a,b\) nonnegative integers, the possible counts of incident angles at any interior vertex are \((a,b)=(8,0),(6,1),(4,2),(2,3),(0,4)\).
At any such interior vertex, the actual number of polygonal edges meeting there is \(a+b\), so it can be \(8,7,6,5,\) or \(4\), respectively.
Since the boundary of the \(1\times 1\) square contributes only \(90^\circ\) angles, any tiling vertex lying on the boundary must have total incident angle a multiple of \(90^\circ\) (again with summands \(45^\circ,90^\circ\)), so for a boundary vertex we have \(45a+90b\in\{90,180,270,360,\dots\}\), hence \(a+2b\in\{2,4,6,8,\dots\}\) and the number of incident polygonal edges there equals \(a+b\in\{2,3,4,5,\dots\}\) with \(a,b\ge 0\).
From \(a+2b=8\) we have \(a=8-2b\), so the incident angle counts \((a,b)\) correspond to \(b=0,1,2,3,4\), giving interior-vertex degrees \(d=a+b=(8-2b)+b=8-b\in\{8,7,6,5,4\}\).
Thus every interior vertex has degree \(d\in\{8,7,6,5,4\}\) (namely \(d=8,7,6,5,4\)), and every boundary vertex has degree at least \(2\); we now use Euler’s formula and double-counting to relate these vertex degrees to the number \(F=8\) of polygonal pieces and the number of edges/vertices of the planar graph.
Let \(V_i\) and \(V_b\) be the numbers of interior and boundary vertices of the planar graph, \(E\) the total number of graph edges, and \(F=8\) the number of pieces (faces); then Euler’s formula gives
\[
V - E + F = 1+\#(\text{components})=2,
\]
so (assuming the tiling graph is connected) \(E=V+F-2=V+6\), and using the degree sum
\[
\sum_{v} \deg(v)=\sum_{v\in \text{interior}} \deg(v)+\sum_{v\in \text{boundary}} \deg(v)=2E=2(V+6).
\]
Using \(\sum_v \deg(v)=2E\), we have
\[
\sum_{v\in \text{interior}}\deg(v)+\sum_{v\in \text{boundary}}\deg(v)=2(V+6)=2V+12,
\]
so equivalently
\[
\sum_{v\in \text{interior}}\deg(v)+\sum_{v\in \text{boundary}}\deg(v)-2V=12.
\]

\[
|S|+|S-a|\le 1000-a+1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2|S|\le 1001-a.
\]
Since \(2|S|\le 1001-a\) and \(a\ge 1\), the maximum occurs at \(a=1\), giving \(2|S|\le 1000\), i.e. \(|S|\le 500\).
Take \(a=1\) and note then \(S\cap(S+1)=\varnothing\), so at most one of each pair \(\{n,n+1\}\subset\{1,\dots,1000\}\) can lie in \(S\); hence \(|S|\le 500\).
With \(a=1\), the condition implies \(S\cap(S+1)=\varnothing\), so among the \(1000\) integers there are \(500\) disjoint pairs \(\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\dots,\{999,1000\}\) and at most one element from each pair can belong to \(S\); hence \(|S|\le 500\).
To achieve \(|S|=500\), take \(S=\{1,3,5,\dots,999\}\), then for any distinct \(x,y\in S\) we have \(x+y\) even and \(\ge 1+3=4\), so \(x+y\notin S\); hence \(|S|=500\) is attainable, giving \(\boxed{500}\).

Let the \(N\)-digit number have digits \(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_N\). The condition “among any sequence of its consecutive decimal digits some digit is present once only” is equivalent to: for every interval \([i,j]\) (\(1\le i\le j\le N\)), there exists \(d\in\{0,\dots,9\}\) such that \(d\) occurs exactly once among \(\{a_i,a_{i+1},\dots,a_j\}\). In particular, applying this to intervals of length \(1\) gives nothing new, while applying it to intervals of length \(2\) yields that no two consecutive digits can be equal, i.e. \(a_k\ne a_{k+1}\) for all \(k\).
Consider an interval of length \(3\), \(\{a_k,a_{k+1},a_{k+2}\}\); since the condition requires some digit to occur exactly once among these three, it is impossible that all three digits are distinct or that two digits occur twice—thus the only allowable pattern (up to relabeling) is \(a_k=a_{k+2}\ne a_{k+1}\), i.e. \(a_k=a_{k+2}\) for every \(k\).
For any \(k\), consider the length-\(4\) interval \((a_k,a_{k+1},a_{k+2},a_{k+3})\); by the length-\(3\) result we have \(a_k=a_{k+2}\) and \(a_{k+1}=a_{k+3}\), so this interval consists of exactly two digits, each appearing twice, hence no digit can occur exactly once—therefore such a number cannot have \(N\ge 4\), i.e. \(N\le 3\).
Check existence for \(N=3\): take digits \(a_1,a_2,a_3\) with \(a_1=a_3\neq a_2\) (e.g. \(101\)); then in every consecutive block of length \(2\) the two digits differ, and in the length-\(3\) block the digit \(a_2\) occurs exactly once, so the property holds. Hence the maximal \(N\) is \(3\), \(\boxed{3}\).

Note that deleting an edge from a 4-cycle reduces the number of edges by 1, so we seek the smallest number of edges that must remain after repeatedly deleting edges that lie on some 4-cycle in \(K_n\).
Observe that an edge can be deleted iff it lies on at least one 4-cycle, so after all possible deletions the remaining graph must have **no** 4-cycle—i.e. it must be a \(C_4\)-free subgraph of \(K_n\) with the **maximum** possible number of edges.
So the minimal number of edges achievable equals the maximum number of edges in a \(C_4\)-free subgraph of \(K_n\). By the extremal result of Kővári–Sós–Turán (for \(C_4\)), this maximum is  
\[
\operatorname{ex}(n,C_4)=\frac12\,n^{3/2}+O(n),
\]
hence the least number of edges obtainable is \(\boxed{\frac12\,n^{3/2}+O(n)}\).

Let us form a bipartite graph with left vertices \(R_1,\dots,R_n\) (rows) and right vertices \(C_1,\dots,C_n\) (columns), and for each pair \((i,j)\) declare an edge between \(R_i\) and \(C_j\) iff \(x_{ij}\) is created by the row (i.e. \(x_{ij}=\max\{x_{i1},\dots,x_{ij}\}\)); then each row \(R_i\) has degree \(\le m\) by (2), each column \(C_j\) has degree \(\le m\) by (3), and every cell \((i,j)\) must be created by exactly one side, so every vertex-set pair \((R_i,C_j)\) is covered by an edge.
Thus we have a bipartite graph on \(n+n\) vertices with maximum degree \(\le m\), and since each of the \(n^2\) cells \((i,j)\) contributes an edge created from either side, the total number of edges is at least \(n^2\); but the total number of edges is also at most \(\sum_{i=1}^n \deg(R_i)\le nm\), hence \(n^2\le nm\) and so \(m\ge n\).
Since each row can “create” at most \(m\) entries and there are \(n\) rows, the number of cells created from the left is \(\le nm\), but every cell must be created from either the left or the top, so the total number of cells \(n^2\) satisfies \(n^2\le nm\), hence \(m\ge n\).
Now we construct an example with \(m=n\): set \(x_{ij}=i+j\) (or \(x_{ij}=i\cdot N+j\) with large base); then in each fixed row \(i\), the running maximum from the left strictly increases at every column \(j\), so condition (2) gives exactly \(n\) “row-creating” indices, and similarly in each fixed column \(j\) the running maximum from the top strictly increases at every row \(i\), so condition (3) gives exactly \(n\) “column-creating” indices. A_i=a_i\ (1\le i\le 20),\qquad C_j=a_{j+20}\ (1\le j\le 20),

Let \(S=\{A_1,\dots,A_{20}\}\) and \(T=\{C_1,\dots,C_{20}\}\). Since \(b_{ij}=\max(A_i,C_j)\), each value \(x\in\{1,\dots,40\}\) appears in the grid exactly according to whether \(x\in S\), \(x\in T\), or both, and the entire grid determines the partition \((S,T)\) up to swapping labels between the two halves; therefore the number of compatible permutations \(a\) equals \(\;2\cdot (20!)^2\) times the number of ways the grid’s forced partition can be realized—so to have exactly \(2\) compatible permutations, the grid must force a unique partition \((S,T)\) with \(S\) and \(T\) each having all distinct values in fixed positions, leaving only the global swap, i.e. \(S\) is determined and \(T\) is the complement.
For exactly 2 compatible permutations, the grid must determine that \(S=\{a_1,\dots,a_{20}\}\) is the set of the 20 largest values \(\{21,22,\dots,40\}\) (and hence \(T=\{1,2,\dots,20\}\)), so among the \(20^2\) comparisons \(b_{ij}=\max(A_i,C_j)\), we must have \(b_{ij}=A_i\) for all \(i,j\) with \(A_i> C_j\), i.e. every \(A_i\) must exceed every \(C_j\); equivalently \(\min(S)>\max(T)\).

\[
\min\{a_1,\dots,a_{20}\}>\max\{a_{21},\dots,a_{40}\}

\{a_1,\dots,a_{20}\}=\{21,22,\dots,40\}.
\]

\[
\frac{\binom{40-20}{0}\binom{20}{20}}{\binom{40}{20}}=\frac{1}{\binom{40}{20}}.
\]
\[
\boxed{\frac{1}{\binom{40}{20}}}

Let \(k=\dfrac{2n}{d}\) and choose \(x=t\,b_1,\ y=t\,(k-a_1)\) with
\[
t=\frac{1}{\***(b_1,k)}\cdot \***\bigl(b_1,k\bigr)\ \Rightarrow\ a_1x+b_1y\equiv 0 \pmod{k},
\]
so one solution has
\[
x+y=t\bigl(b_1+k-a_1\bigr)\le t\,k\le \frac{k}{\***(b_1,k)}\le k.
\]
Let \(d=(a,b)\), \(k=\frac{2n}{d}\). The above construction gives a feasible pair \((x,y)\) with
\[
x+y\le \frac{k}{(b_1,k)}=\frac{2n/d}{\,(b_1,\,2n/d\,)}=\frac{2n}{d\,(b_1,\,2n/d\,)}\le 2n,
\]
so the smallest such \(m\) is \( \boxed{2n} \).

Let \(S\) be the event that you get a prize; since your ticket \(1000\) is even, \(S\) occurs iff the first odd number drawn appears after ticket \(1000\) is drawn, i.e. the process includes all drawn evens up to and including \(1000\) before the first odd.
Since ticket \(1000\) is even, we must have that among the tickets drawn up to the first odd, all are even and the last of them is \(1000\); equivalently, in the random ordering of the \(1000\) tickets, \(1000\) must occur before every odd ticket, and the first odd after it determines the stopping point, so
\[
\Pr(S)=\frac{1}{501}.
\]
Since there are \(500\) odd tickets, and ticket \(1000\) must be the earliest among the \(501\) tickets consisting of \(1000\) and all odd numbers, the probability is \(\displaystyle \boxed{\frac{1}{501}}\).

Let \(x_n=\sqrt{a_n}\) (so \(a_n=x_n^2\)); then the recurrence becomes
\[
x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2=\frac52\,x_n x_{n-1}.
\]
\[
(x_n^2+x_{n-1}^2)^2=\left(\frac52 x_nx_{n-1}\right)^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
x_n^4-5x_n^3x_{n-1}+10x_n^2x_{n-1}^2-5x_nx_{n-1}^3+x_{n-1}^4=0
\;\Rightarrow\;
\left(x_n^2-5x_nx_{n-1}+x_{n-1}^2\right)\left(x_n^2-x_{n-1}^2\right)=0.
\]
Since \(a_n,a_{n-1}>0\), we must have \(x_n^2-5x_nx_{n-1}+x_{n-1}^2=0\), so
\[
\left(\frac{x_n}{x_{n-1}}\right)^2-5\left(\frac{x_n}{x_{n-1}}\right)+1=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{x_n}{x_{n-1}}=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{21}}{2}.
\]
Let \(r=\dfrac{x_n}{x_{n-1}}\), then for each \(n\) we have \(r\in\left\{\dfrac{5+\sqrt{21}}{2},\,\dfrac{5-\sqrt{21}}{2}\right\}\), so
\[
x_n=x_1\prod_{k=2}^{n} r_k
\quad\text{and hence}\quad
a_n=x_n^2=16\prod_{k=2}^{n} r_k^2.
\]
Let \(r_{\pm}=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{21}}{2}\); since \(a_{11}=1024\), we have
\[
1024=a_{11}=16\prod_{k=2}^{11} r_k^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\prod_{k=2}^{11} r_k^2=64
\;\Rightarrow\;
\prod_{k=2}^{11} r_k=\pm 8,
\]
but \(r_\pm>0\), so \(\prod_{k=2}^{11} r_k=8.\)
Since each \(r_k\in\{r_+,r_-\}\) and \(r_+r_-=\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{21}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{5-\sqrt{21}}{2}\right)=\frac{25-21}{4}=1\), if \(m\) of the ratios equal \(r_+\) (and \(10-m\) equal \(r_-\)), then
\[
\prod_{k=2}^{11} r_k = r_+^{m}r_-^{10-m}=r_+^{m} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{r_+}\right)^{10-m}
= r_+^{\,2m-10}=8. \]
\[
r_+^{\,2m-10}=8\ \Rightarrow\ 2m-10=3\ \Rightarrow\ m=\frac{13}{2}\,,
\]
which is impossible, so the remaining factor \(x_n^2-x_{n-1}^2=0\) must be used instead.
So we must have \(x_n^2-x_{n-1}^2=0\), i.e. \(x_n=x_{n-1}\) for all \(n\), hence \(a_n=a_1=4\) for all \(n\), contradicting \(a_{11}=1024\).
Since the factor \(x_n^2-5x_nx_{n-1}+x_{n-1}^2=0\) leads to an impossible counting of \(r_+\) vs. \(r_-\), we instead set \(x_n^2-x_{n-1}^2=0\), i.e. \(x_n=x_{n-1}\) and therefore \(a_n=a_{n-1}\) for all \(n\).

Using \(abc=\frac18\), apply AM-GM:
\[
a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2 \ge 3\sqrt[3]{a^2b^2\cdot b^2c^2\cdot c^2a^2}
=3(abc)^{4/3}=3\left(\frac18\right)^{4/3}=\frac34.
\]
\[
a^2+b^2+c^2 \ge 3\sqrt[3]{a^2b^2c^2}=3(abc)^{2/3}=3\left(\frac18\right)^{2/3}=\frac32,
\]
hence \(a^2+b^2+c^2+a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2 \ge \frac32+\frac34=\frac{9}{4}>\frac{15}{16}\) (equality cannot occur for positive real \(a,b,c\)).
Since the AM–GM equalities require \(a^2=b^2=c^2\), we get \(a=b=c\), and with \(abc=\frac18\) this gives \(a=b=c=\frac12\); but then
\[
a^2+b^2+c^2+a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2=\frac34+\frac34=\frac32,
\]
so equality for the stated bound \(\frac{15}{16}\) does not occur for any positive \(a,b,c\) (the inequality is strict).
Since the minimum obtained by the AM–GM bounds is \(\frac32\) (achieved at \(a=b=c=\tfrac12\)), and \(\frac32>\frac{15}{16}\), the inequality is strict for all positive real \(a,b,c\) with \(abc=\tfrac18\), i.e. **no equality case exists**.
Therefore the inequality is **strict** for all positive \(a,b,c\) with \(abc=\frac18\), i.e. there is **no** equality case.
\[
\boxed{\text{Therefore the inequality is strict for all }a,b,c>0\text{ with }abc=\frac18,\text{ i.e. no equality case occurs.}}
\]

Let \(k=|S|\); then the number of ways to choose \(S\) with the required property equals the total number of subsets minus the subsets with **no** indices \(a<b<c\) having \(a,c\in S\) and \(b\notin S\), i.e. subsets whose elements form at most one contiguous block (so \(S=\varnothing\), or \(S=\{1,\dots,t\}\), or \(S=\{u,\dots,10\}\), or \(S=\{l,\dots,r\}\) with no “gap” inside).
Count the “bad” subsets (with at most one contiguous block) as \(10\) single-block choices for each interval \(\{l,\dots,r\}\) plus \(1\) for the empty set, i.e. \(\binom{10+1}{2}+1=56+1=57\).
\[
\text{Valid subsets}=2^{10}-57=1024-57=967.\quad \boxed{967}
\]

Differentiate \(y=(1+x^{2})^{-1-k}\) to get \(y'=-2(1+k)x(1+x^{2})^{-2-k}\).
\[
y''=-2(1+k)(1+x^2)^{-2-k}-4(1+k)(k+2)x^2(1+x^2)^{-3-k}.
\]
\[
y''=-2(1+k)(1+x^2)^{-2-k}\;-\;4(1+k)(k+2)x^{2}(1+x^2)^{-3-k}
=-2(1+k)(1+x^2)^{-3-k}\bigl(1+x^2+2(k+2)x^2\bigr).
\]
Substitute \(y'=-2(1+k)x(1+x^2)^{-2-k}\) and \(y''=-2(1+k)(1+x^2)^{-3-k}\bigl(1+x^2+2(k+2)x^2\bigr)\) into \(x y''+c_{1}y'+c_{2}xy=0\) and factor out \(x(1+x^2)^{-3-k}\) to get
\[
x(1+x^2)^{-3-k}\Bigl[-2(1+k)\bigl(1+x^2+2(k+2)x^2\bigr)-2c_{1}(1+k)(1+x^2)+c_{2}(1+x^2)^2\Bigr]=0.
\]
Set the bracket to zero and divide by \(-2(1+k)\) (valid for \(k\ge1\)) to get the polynomial identity
\[
\Bigl(1+x^2+2(k+2)x^2\Bigr)+c_{1}(1+x^2)-\frac{c_{2}}{2(1+k)}(1+x^2)^2=0. \]
Match coefficients of \(x^4,x^2,\) and the constant term in
\[
\Bigl(1+(1+2(k+2))x^2\Bigr)+c_{1}(1+x^2)-\frac{c_{2}}{2(1+k)}(1+2x^2+x^4)=0
\]
to get from the \(x^4\) coefficient \(-\dfrac{c_2}{2(1+k)}=0\Rightarrow c_2=0\), hence from the \(x^2\) coefficient \(2k+5+c_1=0\Rightarrow c_1=-(2k+5)\).
Thus \(c_{1}=-(2k+5)\) and \(c_{2}=0\) so the differential equation is \(\boxed{x y''-(2k+5)y'=0}\).

To minimize the largest integer \(n\), take the other three integers as small as possible while keeping them distinct positive integers: \(1,2,3\), so \(n+1+2+3=100\) and \(n=94\).
Check the next possibility: with smallest other three distinct positives \(1,2,4\), we get \(n=100-(1+2+4)=93\), which is smaller than \(94\), so the previous choice was not optimal.
Since \(93<94\), take the next minimal distinct triple \(1,2,5\): \(n=100-(1+2+5)=92\).
Take the next minimal distinct triple \(1,2,6\): \(n=100-(1+2+6)=91\).
Next smallest distinct triple is \(1,2,7\), so \(n=100-(1+2+7)=90\).
Next smallest distinct triple is \(1,2,8\), so \(n=100-(1+2+8)=89\).
Next smallest distinct triple \(1,2,9\) gives \(n=100-(1+2+9)=\boxed{88}\).

Let the ray make angle \(\theta\) with the tangent at \(P\); then its central angle step between successive wall hits is \(2\theta\), so after \(k\) wall hits it returns to \(P\) exactly when \(k\cdot 2\theta\) is a multiple of \(360^\circ\).
For a ray with \(\theta\), the number of distinct wall-hit points until it returns to \(P\) (first time) is \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{\***(360^\circ,\,2\theta)}\).
\[
\text{For }\theta=\frac{n^\circ}{\phantom{1}},\ \text{the return occurs after }k_1=\frac{360}{\***(360,\,2n)}
\text{ wall hits, so the number of illuminated wall points for that ray is }k_1.
\]
Compute the number of illuminated wall points for \(\theta=n^\circ\) as
\[
k_1=\frac{360^\circ}{\***(360^\circ,\,2n^\circ)}.
\]
Compute the ***: \(\***(360,2n)=2\***(180,n)\), so the number of illuminated wall points for \(\theta=n^\circ\) is \(k_1=\dfrac{360}{\***(360,2n)}=\dfrac{360}{2\***(180,n)}=\dfrac{180}{\***(180,n)}\).
For \(\theta=\frac{n+1}{ }\!^\circ\), similarly the number of illuminated wall points is
\[
k_2=\frac{180}{\***(180,n+1)}.
\]
Since the ray first returns to \(P\) when \(k_1\) (resp. \(k_2\)) is minimal positive with \(k_1\cdot 2n\equiv 0\pmod{360}\) (resp. \(k_2\cdot 2(n+1)\equiv 0\pmod{360}\)), we have
\[
k_1=\frac{180}{\***(180,n)}\quad\text{and}\quad k_2=\frac{180}{\***(180,n+1)}.
\]
Thus the minimum possible total number of illuminated wall points equals the minimum over \(1\le n<90\) of
\[
k_1+k_2-\***(k_1,k_2),
\]
because the two rays’ wall-hit sets are cyclic around the room with sizes \(k_1\) and \(k_2\), and their overlap is of size \(\***(k_1,k_2)\).
\[
k_1+k_2-\***(k_1,k_2)
=\frac{180}{\***(180,n)}+\frac{180}{\***(180,n+1)}-\***\!\left(\frac{180}{\***(180,n)},\frac{180}{\***(180,n+1)}\right).
\]
Let \(d=\***(180,n)\) and \(e=\***(180,n+1)\); then \(k_1=\frac{180}{d}\), \(k_2=\frac{180}{e}\), and the overlap size is
\[
\***(k_1,k_2)=\***\!\left(\frac{180}{d},\frac{180}{e}\right)=\frac{180}{\operatorname{lcm}(d,e)}. 
\]

\[
\text{A necessary condition is that every pair }(i,j)\text{ can be swapped, so for all }1\le i<j\le n\text{ we must have }i+j\text{ is a perfect square.}
\]
Since any two positions can be swapped by choosing their current values, we need \(i+j\) to be a perfect square for every unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\), which in particular forces
\[
(n-1)+n=2n-1
\]
to be a perfect square.
Since \(2n-1\) must be a perfect square and \(n>2\), write
\[
2n-1=m^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad n=\frac{m^2+1}{2}.
\]
Since \(n=\frac{m^{2}+1}{2}\) must be an integer, we require \(m^{2}\equiv 1\pmod{2}\), and then imposing the condition for the largest pair \((n-2,n-1)\) gives
\[
(n-2)+(n-1)=2n-3=m^{2}-2 \text{ is a perfect square } \Rightarrow m^{2}-2=k^{2}\text{ for some integer }k.
From \(m^2-2=k^2\), we get \(m^2-k^2=2\), so \((m-k)(m+k)=2\); with integers this forces \(m-k=1\) and \(m+k=2\), hence \(m=\frac{3}{2}\), a contradiction.
The assumption that all pairs \(\{i,j\}\) must be directly swappable is incorrect; thus it is enough to require that, for the graph with vertices \(\{1,\dots,n\}\) and edges \(\{i,j\}\) when \(i+j\) is a perfect square, this graph be connected (so any permutation can be reached via swaps along edges), and the next step is to enforce connectivity starting from the necessary condition \(n+(n-1)=2n-1\) being a square.
Since \(2n-1=m^{2}\), we have \(n=\dfrac{m^{2}+1}{2}\) and the condition \(i+(n-i)=n\) implies the graph has a “complementary” edge whenever \(n\) is a perfect square; in particular, to have any chance of connectivity from the vertex \(n\), we must check when \(n\) itself is a perfect square, so set
\[
n=m^{2}-\ell \quad\text{with}\quad \ell=m^{2}-\frac{m^{2}+1}{2}=\frac{m^{2}-1}{2},
\]
and require \(n=\frac{m^{2}+1}{2}\) to be a perfect square \(=t^{2}\), i.e.
\[
\frac{m^{2}+1}{2}=t^{2}\ \Longrightarrow\ m^{2}-2t^{2}=-1.
\]
From \(\dfrac{m^{2}+1}{2}=t^{2}\) we get \(m^{2}-2t^{2}=-1\), i.e. the negative Pell equation \(m^{2}-2t^{2}=-1\).
Consider \(m^{2}-2t^{2}=-1\). Modulo \(8\), squares are \(0,1,4\), and \(2t^{2}\equiv 0,2\pmod 8\), so \(m^{2}-2t^{2}\equiv -1\pmod 8\) forces \(m^{2}\equiv 1\pmod 8\) and \(2t^{2}\equiv 2\pmod 8\), hence \(t\) is odd.

Since the expression is cyclic and homogeneous, let \(b=a x\), \(c=a x y\) with \(1\le x\le xy\le 2\); then
\[
\frac{b}{a}+\frac{c}{b}+\frac{a}{c}=x+y+\frac1{xy}.
\]
Let \(p=xy\) (so \(1\le p\le 2\) and \(x\in[1,p]\)); then for fixed \(p\),
\[
x+y+\frac1{xy}=x+\frac{p}{x}+\frac1p
\]
is maximized at an endpoint \(x=1\) or \(x=p\), giving
\[
\max_{1\le x\le p}\left(x+\frac{p}{x}+\frac1p\right)=p+1+\frac1p.
\]
Now maximize \(p+1+\frac{1}{p}\) over \(1\le p\le 2\), which is increasing since \(\frac{d}{dp}\left(p+\frac1p\right)=1-\frac1{p^2}\ge0\), so the maximum occurs at \(p=2\), giving \(2+1+\frac12=\boxed{\frac{7}{2}}\).

Since \(2p+3q=6r\), the left side is divisible by \(3\), so \(2p\equiv 0\pmod 3\), hence \(p=3\).
\[
2p+3q=6r \ \Rightarrow\ 2\cdot 3+3q=6r \ \Rightarrow\ 6(1+q)=6r \ \Rightarrow\ r=q+1.
\]
Since \(r=q+1\) and \(q,r\) are primes, \(q\) must be \(2\), so \(r=3\) and therefore \(p+q+r=3+2+3=8\), i.e. \(\boxed{8}\).

Let \(S_k=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^k\). Then the given conditions are
\[
-S_1=1,\quad -S_2=1,\ \ldots,\ -S_{n-1}=1,\quad -S_n=2,\quad -S_m=4,
\]
i.e.
\[
S_k=-1\ (1\le k\le n-1),\qquad S_n=-2,\qquad S_m=-4.
\]
Consider the polynomial \(P(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n (t-x_i)\) and let \(e_j\) be its elementary symmetric sums; then Newton’s identities imply
\[
S_k-e_1 S_{k-1}+e_2 S_{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}e_{k-1}S_1+(-1)^k k e_k=0\quad (1\le k\le n-1),
\]
so with \(S_1=\cdots=S_{n-1}=-1\) we get a unique sequence \((e_1,\dots,e_{n-1})\) and hence determine \(P(t)\) up to the remaining parameter fixed by \(S_n=-2\), i.e. \(P(t)\) must equal \(t^{n}+t^{n-1}+\cdots+t+2\).
Using \(P(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n (t-x_i)=t^{n}+t^{n-1}+\cdots+t+2\), we have \(x_i\) are roots of \(P\), so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^m = -\text{coeff}_{t^{n-m}}\bigl(t^n+t^{n-1}+\cdots+t+2\bigr)\ \Rightarrow\ S_m=-(1+1+\cdots+1\text{ ($m-n$ terms)})=-\bigl(m-(n-1)\bigr)=-\bigl(m-n+1\bigr),
\]
hence \(-\bigl(m-n+1\bigr)= -4\), giving \(m-n=3\).
Thus the conditions force \(m=n+3\), so the smallest possible value of \(m+n\) occurs when \(n\) is minimal (namely \(n=2\)), giving \(\boxed{m+n=(n+3)+n=7}\).

\[
p_f=\tfrac13\bigl(1+p_g\bigr)+\tfrac13\bigl(0+p_w\bigr)+\tfrac13\bigl(0+ p_g\bigr)
\]
(so we condition on Gary playing \(F,G,W\) against Ash’s \(F\)).
\[
p_f=\frac13(1+p_g)+\frac13p_w+\frac13p_g=\frac13+\frac{2}{3}p_g+\frac13 p_w.
\]
\[
p_g=\tfrac13 p_f+\tfrac13(1+p_w)+\tfrac13 p_f=\tfrac13+\tfrac13 p_w+\tfrac23 p_f.
\]
\[
p_w=\tfrac13\bigl(1+p_f\bigr)+\tfrac13 p_g+\tfrac13 p_f=\tfrac13+\tfrac23 p_f+\tfrac13 p_g.
\]

p_g= \frac{5}{13}+\frac{16}{13}p_f.

p_f=\frac{26}{39}+\frac{20}{39}p_f \;\Rightarrow\; p_f=\frac{26}{19}.

Since there is exactly one perfect matching in the bipartite graph, the maximal number of suitable edges occurs when every non-matching edge would create an alternative perfect matching, so the maximum is obtained by making all edges incident to the forced matching neighbors except those that would permit a second perfect matching, giving \(n^2-n+1\).
Let \(M\) be the unique perfect matching, so every edge not in \(M\) must be “forbidden” in the sense that adding it would create a second perfect matching; for a fixed edge \(e=(G_i,B_j)\notin M\), the cycle in \(M\cup\{e\}\) has length \(2k\ge 4\), and to prevent a second perfect matching we must delete at least one of the \(k-1\) other edges on that cycle, implying at most one extra edge can be added per matching edge beyond the \(n\) edges of \(M\), hence the maximum total number of suitable pairs is \(\boxed{n^2-n+1}\).

Let the actual thief be \(T\in\{1,2,3\}\), and let each musketeer \(i\) make one of the \(6\) statements: \(\text{“}j\text{ is guilty”}\) for some \(j\), or \(\text{“}j\text{ is innocent”}\) for some \(j\neq i\); then a statement is true iff it matches \(T\), and since exactly one musketeer lied, among the three made statements exactly two are true (so the statement about the guilty \(T\) is true) and one is false.
Fix the thief \(T\). For any ordered triple of statements to be consistent with “exactly one lied,” we must have:
- one musketeer says “\(T\) is guilty” (a true statement),
- the other two musketeers say statements that are false (so each must name a person other than \(T\) as guilty, since any statement naming \(T\) as innocent would be true, and any statement naming someone other than the speaker as guilty/innocent can be checked similarly),
so the only valid patterns are: choose which musketeer makes the true “\(T\) is guilty” statement (\(3\) choices), and then each of the remaining two musketeers has exactly \(2\) false options for their named person (among the two not equal to \(T\)); hence for this fixed \(T\) there are \(3\cdot 2^2=12\) ordered statement triplets.
Since \(T\) can be any of the \(3\) musketeers and (by the “exactly one lied” condition) each such choice contributes \(12\) consistent ordered statement triplets, the total number is \(3\cdot 12=36\), i.e. \(\boxed{36}\).

Consider the behavior modulo \(100\): the last two digits of \(a^{2^n}\) stabilize iff \(a^{2^n}\) is eventually constant mod \(100\), i.e. iff for some \(N\) we have \(a^{2^{n+1}}\equiv a^{2^n}\pmod{100}\) for all \(n\ge N\), equivalently \(a^{2^n}(a^{2^n}-1)\equiv 0\pmod{100}\) for all \(n\ge N\).
We need eventual constancy mod \(100=4\cdot 25\), so it suffices to require stabilization modulo \(4\) and modulo \(25\) separately.
Work modulo \(25\): since \(\varphi(25)=20\), for any \(a\) with \(\***(a,25)=1\) we have \(a^{2^n}\) periodic mod \(25\); thus eventual constancy requires that the sequence becomes fixed, so for some \(n\ge N\),
\[
a^{2^{n+1}}\equiv a^{2^n}\pmod{25}\iff a^{2^n}(a^{2^n}-1)\equiv 0\pmod{25},
\]
and because \(\***(a,25)=1\) this reduces to \(a^{2^n}\equiv 1\pmod{25}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), i.e. \(2^n\) is eventually always a multiple of \(\operatorname{ord}_{25}(a)\), which happens iff \(\operatorname{ord}_{25}(a)\) is a power of \(2\); among the divisors of \(20=2^2\cdot 5\), only \(1,2,4\) qualify.
So we require \(\operatorname{ord}_{25}(a)\in\{1,2,4\}\), i.e. \(a^{1}\equiv1,\ a^{2}\equiv1,\) or \(a^{4}\equiv1\pmod{25}\), which is equivalent to \(a^{4}\equiv1\pmod{25}\) with order not equal to \(5\) or \(20\).
So we count \(a\) with \(2\le a\le 101\) satisfying
\[
a^{4}\equiv 1 \pmod{25}\quad(\text{and } \operatorname{ord}_{25}(a)\ne 5,20),
\]
i.e. solving \(x^4\equiv 1\pmod{25}\) and then excluding those with \(x^5\equiv1\pmod{25}\) but \(x\not\equiv1\pmod{25}\).
\[
x^4\equiv 1 \pmod{25}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ x^4-1=(x^2-1)(x^2+1)\equiv 0\pmod{25},
\]
so we solve separately \(x^2\equiv 1\pmod{25}\) and \(x^2\equiv -1\pmod{25}\).
Solve \(x^2\equiv 1\pmod{25}\): since \((x-1)(x+1)\equiv 0\pmod{25}\) and \(\***(x-1,x+1)\mid 2\), the only possibilities are \(x\equiv 1\pmod{25}\) or \(x\equiv -1\pmod{25}\), giving \(x\equiv 1,24\pmod{25}\) (2 solutions).
Now solve \(x^2\equiv -1\pmod{25}\).
Solve \(x^2\equiv -1\pmod{25}\) by lifting from mod \(5\): since \(x^2\equiv -1\equiv 4\pmod{5}\), we have \(x\equiv \pm 2\pmod{5}\).  
Set \(x=5k\pm2\) and impose \((5k\pm2)^2+1\equiv 0\pmod{25}\):
\[
(5k+2)^2+1=25k^2+20k+5=5(5k^2+4k+1)\equiv 0\pmod{25}
\]
so \(5k^2+4k+1\equiv 0\pmod{5}\), i.e. \(4k+1\equiv 0\pmod{5}\), hence \(k\equiv 1\pmod{5}\) and \(x\equiv 5\cdot1+2=7\pmod{25}\).  
Similarly,
\[
(5k-2)^2+1=25k^2-20k+5=5(5k^2-4k+1)\equiv 0\pmod{25}
\]
so \(-4k+1\equiv 0\pmod{5}\), giving \(k\equiv 1\pmod{5}\) and \(x\equiv 5\cdot1-2=3\pmod{25}\).

Observe that for integer \(n\), \(\lfloor n/k\rfloor\) is the largest integer \(\le n/k\), so \(f(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor\) is odd iff the sum of these integers has odd parity.
Compute \(f(n)\pmod 2\): since \(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor\) is odd exactly when \(\frac{n}{k}\in [2m+1,2m+2)\), the parity of \(f(n)\) equals the parity of the count of integers \(k\) for which \(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor\) is odd.
Let \(a=\left\lfloor \frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor\); then \(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{k}\right\rfloor\) is odd exactly for those \(k\) with \(2m+1\le \frac{n}{k}<2m+2\), i.e. 
\[
\frac{n}{2m+2}<k\le \frac{n}{2m+1},
\]
so the number of such \(k\) equals \(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2m+1}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2m+2}\right\rfloor\), and therefore
\[
f(n)\equiv \sum_{m\ge 0}\left(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2m+1}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2m+2}\right\rfloor\right)\pmod 2. \]

\[

\equiv \sum_{m\ge0}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2m+1}\right\rfloor-\sum_{m\ge0}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2m+2}\right\rfloor
\equiv \sum_{j=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{j}\right\rfloor \cdot(-1)^{j+1}\pmod 2, 
\]
so \(f(n)\) is odd iff \(\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{j}\right\rfloor(-1)^{j+1}\) is odd.
Compute the parity directly by pairing terms \(j\) and \(2j\): for \(j\ge1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{n}{j}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2j}\right\rfloor=\sum_{t=0}^{1}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2^t j}\right\rfloor(-1)^{t}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{j}\right\rfloor(-1)^{j+1}\equiv \sum_{\substack{j\le n\\ j\ \text{odd}}}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{j}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2j}\right\rfloor\pmod 2,
\]
so \(f(n)\) is odd iff \(\displaystyle \sum_{\substack{j\le n\\ j\ \text{odd}}}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{j}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2j}\right\rfloor\right)\) is odd.

\[

\]
hence \(f(n)\) is odd iff the number of odd \(j\le n\) for which \(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{j}\right\rfloor\equiv 2,3\pmod 4\) is odd.
\[

\]

\[

\]

\]

Let the unit square have vertices \((0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)\), and place \(X=(t,0),\,Y=(1-t,1)\) so that each vertex is closest to exactly one of \(X,Y\); then the four scores sum to
\[

\[

Since \(ax^2+bx+c\) has integer roots, its discriminant must be a perfect square: \(b^2-4ac=k^2\) for some integer \(k\), i.e.
\[
b^2-4ac=k^2.\]
For \(ax^2+bx-c\) the discriminant is \(b^2+4ac\), so \(b^2+4ac=\ell^2\) for some integer \(\ell\), hence subtracting gives \(\ell^2-k^2=8ac\).
\[
\ell^2-k^2=(\ell-k)(\ell+k)=8ac.\]
Since \((\ell-k)(\ell+k)=8ac\) and \(\ell\pm k\) have the same parity, both \(\ell-k\) and \(\ell+k\) must be even; let \(\ell-k=2r,\ \ell+k=2s\) with \(r,s\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), giving \(ac=rs\) and \(\ell^2-k^2=4(s^2-r^2)=8ac\Rightarrow s^2-r^2=2rs\Rightarrow (s-r)^2=2r^2\), so \(\frac{s}{r}=1+\sqrt2\), which is impossible over integers unless \(r=0\); therefore we must instead enforce integrality via the other pair discriminants.
Because all four quadratics have integer roots, in particular
\[
ax^2+bx+c\ \text{and}\ ax^2-bx+c
\]
must both have discriminant perfect squares, so with
\[
b^2-4ac=k^2,\qquad (-b)^2-4ac=k'^2
\]
we get the same condition twice, and similarly
\[
b^2+4ac=\ell^2
\]
must hold; hence
\[
(b^2+4ac)-(b^2-4ac)=8ac=\ell^2-k^2=(\ell-k)(\ell+k),
\]
so \(\ell-k\) and \(\ell+k\) are positive even integers whose product is \(8ac\), i.e. write \(\ell-k=2m,\ \ell+k=4n\) with \(mn=ac\).
Let \(\ell-k=2m\) and \(\ell+k=4n\) with \(m,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). Then
\[
8ac=(\ell-k)(\ell+k)=(2m)(4n)=8mn\quad\Rightarrow\quad ac=mn.
\]
Since \(b^2+4ac=\ell^2\) and \(\ell-k=2m,\ \ell+k=4n\), we have \(\ell^2=(\ell+k)(\ell-k)=(4n)(2m)=8mn\), so
\[
b^2+4ac=\ell^2=8mn \quad\Rightarrow\quad b^2+4mn=8mn \quad\Rightarrow\quad b^2=4mn=4ac.
\]
Since \(b^2=4ac\), we have \((b/2)^2=ac\), so \(b\) must be even; let \(b=2d\). Then \(d^2=ac\).
Since \(d^2=ac\) with \(a,c\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), we must have \(a=d u,\ c=d/u\) for some positive integer \(u\) with \(u\mid d\); i.e. \(a=du,\ c=dv\) where \(uv=1\), so \(u\) and \(v\) are reciprocal and hence the only possibility is \(a=c=d\).

\[

\[
\bigl(n-1-n^2C_n\bigr)(x^2+y^2)+\bigl(2n^2C_n-2\bigr)xy
\]

\]

Let \(f(n,s)\) be the maximum achievable probability of eventually ending with exactly \(s\) points when there are \(n\) marbles remaining and the current score is \(s\); then the first decision (keep/pass) yields the recursion
\[
f(n,s)=\tfrac12\,f(n-1,s+3)+\tfrac12\,f(n-1,s-2)\;\;+\;\;\tfrac12\,g_{\text{pass}}(n-1,s),
\]
with \(g_{\text{pass}}(n-1,s)=f(n-1,s)\) corresponding to choosing “pass,” so
\[
f(n,s)=\max\Big\{\,\tfrac12 f(n-1,s+3)+\tfrac12 f(n-1,s-2),\; f(n-1,s)\Big\}.
\]
Let \(p(n,s)\) be the *maximum* probability of eventually reaching exactly 1 point starting from \((n,s)\); then
\[
p(n,s)=\max\!\left\{\tfrac12\,p(n-1,s+3)+\tfrac12\,p(n-1,s-2),\;p(n-1,s)\right\},
\quad
p(0,s)=\mathbf{1}_{\{s=1\}}.
\]
\[
p(n,s)=
\max\!\left\{\tfrac12\,p(n-1,s+3)+\tfrac12\,p(n-1,s-2),\;p(n-1,s)\right\}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{p(n,s)\ge p(n-1,s)\ \text{for all }n,s,\ \text{so passing is never better than (or equal to) taking the conditional expectation.}
}

Let \(a_1=\frac m2\). For \(a_2=a_1\lceil a_1\rceil\) to be an integer, we must have \(\lceil a_1\rceil\in\mathbb Z\) (always) and \(\frac m2\cdot \lceil \frac m2\rceil\in\mathbb Z\), which forces \(m\) to be even so that \(a_1\in\mathbb Z\); hence the first integer can occur only when \(\frac m2\notin\mathbb Z\) is impossible and we proceed with \(m\) odd being the only way \(a_1\) is non-integer.
Since \(a_1=\dfrac m2\), for the first integer to appear at the term \(a_{2007}\) we must have \(a_1\notin\mathbb Z\), so \(m\) is odd, and then \(a_{n+1}=a_n\lceil a_n\rceil\) implies \(a_n=\dfrac{m}{2}\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\lceil a_k\rceil\) with \(\lceil a_k\rceil\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(k\), so the denominator of \(a_n\) is always \(2\); thus \(a_n\) can be an integer only when \(\lceil a_{n-1}\rceil\) is even.
Since \(m\) is odd, \(a_1=\dfrac m2\) is half-integer, so \(\lceil a_1\rceil=\dfrac{m+1}{2}\) is an integer. For the first integer to occur at \(a_{2007}\), we need \(\lceil a_{k}\rceil\) to be odd for all \(k=1,2,\dots,2005\) (so that the factor \(\lceil a_k\rceil\) never cancels the remaining denominator \(2\)), while \(\lceil a_{2006}\rceil\) must be even so that multiplying by it makes \(a_{2007}\) an integer.
Since \(a_{n+1}=a_n\lceil a_n\rceil\) and for \(m\) odd we have \(a_1=\frac m2\) a half-integer, we have \(\lceil a_1\rceil=\frac{m+1}{2}\); therefore
\[
\lceil a_k\rceil \text{ is odd for } k=1,\dots,2005 \iff \frac{m+1}{2}\cdot 2^{k-1}\not\equiv 0\pmod 2,
\]
so the condition becomes \(\frac{m+1}{2}\) odd (i.e. \(m\equiv 1\pmod 4\)) for all those early terms, while \(\lceil a_{2006}\rceil\) even forces \(m\equiv 3\pmod 4\), contradiction; hence no such \(m\) exists.
This contradiction shows there is **no** integer \(m\) for which \(a_{2007}\) is the first integer appearing in the sequence, so the set of all such \(m\) is \(\boxed{\varnothing}\).

Since \(ax+y\equiv k\pmod{37}\) must hold for every \(k\in\{1,\dots,36\}\), the set \(\{ax+y\bmod 37:\ x,y\in X\}\subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{37}\) must equal all nonzero residues, i.e. must have at least \(36\) distinct values modulo \(37\).
Since there are at most \(6\cdot 6=36\) ordered pairs \((x,y)\in X\times X\), achieving all \(36\) nonzero residues mod \(37\) implies that the \(36\) values \(ax+y \pmod{37}\) are pairwise distinct, so in particular the map
\[
(x,y)\mapsto ax+y \pmod{37}
\]
from \(X\times X\) onto \(\mathbb{Z}_{37}^\*\) is a bijection, hence for any fixed \(y\in X\) the six residues \(\{ax+y:\ x\in X\}\) must be all distinct mod \(37\).
Fix any \(y\in X\). The condition implies the residues \(\{ax+y \pmod{37}: x\in X\}\) must be \(6\) distinct nonzero classes, so in particular the map \(x\mapsto ax+y\pmod{37}\) is injective on \(X\); hence \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod{37}\).
Since for some fixed \(y\in X\) the six residues \(\{ax+y \pmod{37}:x\in X\}\) are distinct, we have \(ax_1+y\equiv ax_2+y\pmod{37}\Rightarrow x_1\equiv x_2\pmod{37}\); thus the reduction of \(X\) modulo \(37\) consists of six distinct residues.
For any fixed \(y\in X\), since the residues \(\{ax+y \bmod 37:\ x\in X\}\) are \(6\) distinct nonzero classes, it follows that \(a\) is invertible mod \(37\) (so \(a\not\equiv0\pmod{37}\)) and therefore the residues \(\{ax \bmod 37:\ x\in X\}\) are exactly the six distinct nonzero classes; hence \(X\) reduces modulo \(37\) to a set of \(6\) distinct nonzero residues and \(aX\) is just a permutation of them in \(\mathbb Z_{37}^\*\).
Since for each \(k\in\{1,\dots,36\}\) there must be \(x,y\in X\) with \(ax+y\equiv k\pmod{37}\), the set of all differences
\[
(ax_1+y)-(ax_2+y)=a(x_1-x_2)\pmod{37}
\]
as \(x_1\neq x_2\) and \(y\in X\) must cover all nonzero residues; in particular the set of differences \(\{x_1-x_2: x_1\neq x_2,\ x_1,x_2\in X\}\) must have size \(6\choose2\cdot 2=30\) and therefore must equal \(\mathbb Z_{37}^\*\) minus exactly the 6 residues corresponding to differences between elements mapping to the same residue under the bijection, forcing \(a\equiv 1\pmod{37}\).

\[
a^3+b^3=(2+\sqrt5)+(2-\sqrt5)=4,\qquad ab=\sqrt[3]{(2+\sqrt5)(2-\sqrt5)}=\sqrt[3]{-1}=-1.
\]
\[
(a+b)^3=a^3+b^3+3ab(a+b)=4-3(a+b)\;\Rightarrow\; (a+b)^3+3(a+b)-4=0. 
\]
\[
(a+b)^3+3(a+b)-4=0\ \Rightarrow\ (a+b-1)( (a+b)^2+(a+b)+4)=0\ \Rightarrow\ a+b=1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sqrt[3]{2+\sqrt5}+\sqrt[3]{2-\sqrt5}=a+b=1=\boxed{1}.
\]

Let the final configuration (after 2012 cars) be determined by the greedy “maximize the minimal distance” rule; to force the last car to choose spot \(1\), spot \(1\) must be the only remaining spot (at the last step) whose distance to the nearest already-occupied spot equals the maximal possible minimal distance among remaining spots.
Let \(d\) be the maximal minimal distance achievable by the last car among the remaining unoccupied spots; then for the last car to be forced to choose spot \(1\), spot \(1\) must be the **unique** remaining spot whose distance to the nearest occupied spot equals \(d\) (so all other remaining spots have smaller nearest-occupied distance).
Let the greedy placements create a set of occupied spots, and at the last step let \(S\) be the remaining unoccupied spots; define for each \(s\in S\) the quantity \(f(s)=\min\{|s-a|:a\ \text{occupied}\}\), then the last car is forced to choose spot \(1\) iff \(f(1)=\max_{s\in S} f(s)\) and \(f(s)<f(1)\) for every \(s\in S\setminus\{1\}\).
Let \(S\) be the remaining unoccupied set when one car remains, and let \(f(s)=\min\{|s-a|:a\text{ occupied}\}\); then the last car is forced to choose spot \(1\) **iff**
\[
f(1)=\max_{s\in S} f(s)\quad\text{and}\quad f(s)\le f(1)-1\ \text{for all }s\in S\setminus\{1\}.
\]
At the final stage with one car left, the maximal minimal distance among remaining spots is exactly the distance from spot \(1\) to the nearest occupied spot (so if the last choice is forced to be spot \(1\), then the nearest occupied spot to \(1\) must be at some position \(m\) such that every other remaining spot lies strictly closer—by at least \(1\)—to the occupied set than \(1\) does.
At the second-to-last step there are exactly two unoccupied spots; for the last car to be *forced* to choose spot \(1\), the other remaining unoccupied spot \(j\neq 1\) must satisfy that its distance to the nearest occupied spot is strictly smaller than spot \(1\)’s distance, i.e.
\[
\min\{|j-a|:a\in\text{(occupied)}\}\le \min\{|1-a|:a\in\text{(occupied)}\}-1.
\]
At the penultimate step (with exactly two unoccupied spots \(1\) and \(j\)), spot \(1\) is forced at the last step iff
\[
d_j:=\min\{|j-a|:a\ \text{occupied}\}\;<\;d_1:=\min\{|1-a|:a\ \text{occupied}\},
\]
equivalently iff \(d_j\le d_1-1\).
At the penultimate step there are two adjacent unoccupied spots \(1\) and \(j\) (with \(j>1\)), so \(d_1=\min\{a-1: a \text{ occupied}\}\) is the distance from spot \(1\) to the nearest occupied spot to its right, while \(d_j=\min\{|j-a|:a\text{ occupied}\}\) is the distance from \(j\) to the nearest occupied spot, which is at most \(d_j\le j-1\); therefore the forcing condition \(d_j\le d_1-1\) can hold only if \(j=2\) and the nearest occupied spot to the left of \(2\) is actually spot \(3\), i.e. the configuration must be such that at the second-to-last step the only unoccupied spots are \(\{1,2\}\).
At the second-to-last step, the only unoccupied spots must therefore be \(\{1,2\}\), so the penultimate car must park in spot \(3\) (the unique spot available that leaves exactly \(\{1,2\}\) empty).

Let \(p_k\) be the probability rain happens exactly \(k\) days from today; with \(p_0=0\), \(p_{k+1}=0.75\,p_k+0.25(1-p_k)=0.25+0.5p_k\), so \(p_k=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\left(\tfrac12\right)^k\).
We need \(P(\text{rain by day }n)=\sum_{k=1}^n p_k = \sum_{k=1}^n \left(\tfrac12-\tfrac12\left(\tfrac12\right)^k\right)=\tfrac n2-\tfrac12\sum_{k=1}^n\left(\tfrac12\right)^k=\tfrac n2-\tfrac12\cdot\frac{\tfrac12\left(1-\left(\tfrac12\right)^n\right)}{1-\tfrac12}= \tfrac n2-\tfrac12\left(1-\left(\tfrac12\right)^n\right)\, .
We require \(\frac n2-\frac12\left(1-\left(\frac12\right)^n\right)>0.499\), i.e. \(n-\left(1-\left(\frac12\right)^n\right)>0.998\), so \(n>1.998-\left(\frac12\right)^n\) and checking \(n=2\): \(1+\left(\frac12\right)^2=1.25>0.499\Rightarrow n\) is at least \(2\).
Evaluate \(n=2\): \(P(\text{rain by day }2)=\left(\frac{2}{2}\right)-\frac12\left(1-\left(\frac12\right)^2\right)=1-\frac12\left(1-\frac14\right)=1-\frac38=0.625>0.499\), so the smallest positive integer is \(\boxed{2}\).

Note that \(a_{1000}-a_1 \equiv a_{1000} \pmod{100}\) since \(a_1=2^{n}\) and \(100\mid (2^{a_{999}}-2^{n})\) will be checked via congruences modulo \(4\) and \(25\).
Since \(a_{1}=2^{n}\) and \(a_{k+1}=2^{a_k}\), we have \(a_{1000}-a_1\equiv a_{1000}\pmod{100}\), so we require
\[
100\mid a_{1000}\iff 4\mid a_{1000}\ \text{and}\ 25\mid a_{1000}.
\]
Since \(a_{1000}=2^{a_{999}}\) is a power of \(2\), we have \(4\mid a_{1000}\iff a_{999}\ge 2\), which holds for all \(n\ge 1\), so it remains only to impose \(25\mid 2^{a_{999}} \iff 2^{a_{999}}\equiv 0 \pmod{25}\), i.e. \(a_{999}\equiv 0 \pmod{20}\).
Thus we need \(a_{999}\equiv 0\pmod{20}\), i.e. \(2^{a_{998}} \equiv 0 \pmod{20}\).
We require \(a_{998}\ge 2\), so modulo \(20=4\cdot5\) we have \(5\mid 2^{a_{999}}\) and thus \(2^{a_{998}}\equiv 0\pmod5\), i.e. \(a_{998}\equiv 0\pmod4\).
Imposing \(a_{998}\equiv 0 \pmod 4\) and continuing similarly gives that the needed condition is \(a_{k}\equiv 0\pmod{20}\) with \(k=999\), so \(a_{999}\equiv 0\pmod{20}\iff a_0=n\equiv 0\pmod{20}\).
\[

\boxed{50}
\]

\]

Let \(S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n f(k)\); then \(S_n\) is a perfect square for every \(n\), so write \(S_n=a_n^2\) with \(a_n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), hence
\[
f(n)=S_n-S_{n-1}=a_n^2-a_{n-1}^2=(a_n-a_{n-1})(a_n+a_{n-1}).
\]
Since \(f(n)=a_n^2-a_{n-1}^2=(a_n-a_{n-1})(a_n+a_{n-1})\mid n^3\), we must have
\[
a_n-a_{n-1}\mid n^3\quad \text{and}\quad a_n+a_{n-1}\mid n^3.
\]
Since \((a_n-a_{n-1})\) and \((a_n+a_{n-1})\) have the same parity, their product
\[
f(n)=(a_n-a_{n-1})(a_n+a_{n-1})\mid n^3
\]
forces the quotient possibilities
\[
a_n-a_{n-1}\in\{1,n,n^2,n^3\},\quad a_n+a_{n-1}\in\left\{ \frac{n^3}{1},\frac{n^3}{n},\frac{n^3}{n^2},\frac{n^3}{n^3}\right\},
\]
so in particular \(a_n-a_{n-1}\le n^3\) and \(a_n+a_{n-1}\le n^3\), hence \(a_n\le n^3\).
From \(a_n^2=S_n\) and \(a_n-a_{n-1}\ge 1\), we get \(a_n\ge n\), and with \(a_n\le n^3\) we refine using
\[
a_n^2-a_{n-1}^2=f(n)\mid n^3\ \Rightarrow\ a_n^2\equiv a_{n-1}^2\pmod{n^3},
\]
so \((a_n-a_{n-1})(a_n+a_{n-1})\equiv 0\pmod{n^3}\); since both factors are positive and \(a_n-a_{n-1}\le n^3,\ a_n+a_{n-1}\le n^3\), the only way their product is divisible by \(n^3\) is
\[
(a_n-a_{n-1})(a_n+a_{n-1})=n^3,
\]
i.e. \(f(n)=n^3\).
Since \(f(n)\mid n^3\) and the congruence forces \((a_n-a_{n-1})(a_n+a_{n-1})=n^3\), we conclude \(f(n)=n^3\) for every \(n\) (so \(S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n k^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2\) is a perfect square).
Therefore the only possible increment is \(a_n-a_{n-1}=n^3\) and \(a_n+a_{n-1}=1\), giving \(2a_n=n^3+1\), hence \(f(n)=a_n^2-a_{n-1}^2=n^3\) for all \(n\). \(\boxed{f(n)=n^3}\)

Let \(p>N\) be a prime with \(f(p)>0\) and set \(m=f(p)\); then the condition gives
\[
p\mid 2(m!)+1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2(m!)+1\equiv 0 \pmod p,
\]
so in particular \(p\neq 2\) and hence \(p\le 2(m!)\!+\!1\), which implies \(p\le m\) or else \(p>m\) would force \(m!\not\equiv 0\pmod p\) and lead to a contradiction with the fixed “\(+1\)” residue.
Since \(p\le 2(m!)+1\), if \(p>m\) then \(m!\not\equiv 0\pmod p\), so \(2(m!)\equiv -1\pmod p\) implies \(p\mid (2(m!)^2-1)\); but for \(p>m\) we have \((m!)^2<(p/2)^2<p^2\), hence \(0<2(m!)^2-1<p^2\) so the only way \(p\) can divide it is \(2(m!)^2-1=0\), impossible for integer \(m\ge1\); therefore we must have \(p\le m\), i.e. \(f(p)\ge p\) for all primes \(p>N\).
Since the condition must hold for all primes \(p>N\) with \(f(p)>0\), we now have \(p\le f(p)\) for every such prime, so in particular \(f(p)\ge p\) for infinitely many primes; comparing degrees in the monic polynomial \(f(x)\), this forces \(\deg f=1\), hence \(f(x)=x+c\) for some integer \(c\).
\[
\text{Let }f(x)=x+c\text{ with }c\in\mathbb Z;\ \text{for primes }p>N\text{ we have }m=f(p)=p+c\ge1,\text{ so }p\mid 2((p+c)!)+1.
\]
Since this must hold for all sufficiently large primes with \(p+c\ge 1\), in particular take primes \(p>N\) so large that \(p+c>0\); then the condition becomes
\[
p \mid 2\big((p+c)!\big)+1 \quad \text{for all such primes }p.
\]
Let \(p\) be a prime \(>N\) with \(p>|c|\) and \(p+c>0\); then \(p\le p+c\) so \(p\mid (p+c)!\), hence \((p+c)!\equiv 0\pmod p\) and the condition gives
\[
2((p+c)!)+1\equiv 0+1\equiv 1 \pmod p,
\]
impossible. Therefore no such primes can exist unless \(c\) makes \(p\nmid (p+c)!\) for all sufficiently large \(p\).
Thus for any integer \(c\), if \(p>|c|\) then \(p+c\ge p\) so \(p\mid (p+c)!\), giving \(2((p+c)!)+1\equiv 1\pmod p\), a contradiction; hence there are no monic integer-coefficient polynomials satisfying the condition. \(\boxed{\text{No such polynomial exists}}\)

Since a primitive dinosaur has at least 2007 cells but cannot be partitioned into two dinosaurs, its cell set must be connected and must remain connected after removing any single “bridge” cut that would separate it into two parts each of size at least 2007; in particular, the only way to avoid such a partition is for the figure to have tree-like (no cycle) adjacency graph, so its adjacency graph is a tree.
Since the adjacency graph is a tree with at least \(2007\) vertices and each tree on \(N\) vertices has a leaf, removing a leaf produces a connected subanimal with \(N-1\) cells; thus if \(N\ge 2\cdot 2007=4014\), we can remove a suitable set of leaves (or equivalently take a connected subtree of size \(2007\)) to partition the dinosaur into two dinosaurs, so primitiveness forces \(N\le 4013\).
Therefore the adjacency graph of a primitive dinosaur must be a tree with \(N\le 4013\), and it remains to show that every such tree with \(4013\) cells is indeed primitive.
Let \(T\) be any tree on \(N\le 4013\) cells, and suppose we try to partition its vertex set into two (connected) subanimals \(A\) and \(B\) with \(|A|,|B|\ge 2007\); let \(e\) be the unique edge of \(T\) between \(A\) and \(B\), so removing \(e\) splits \(T\) into two components of sizes \(|A|\) and \(|B|\), whose sizes therefore sum to \(N\ge 4014\), contradicting \(N\le 4013\). Hence no such partition exists, so \(T\) is primitive.
Thus the maximum number of cells in a primitive dinosaur is the largest \(N\) for which a tree adjacency graph is possible without allowing a split into two connected parts of size \(\ge 2007\), namely \(N=4013\), so \(\boxed{4013}\).

Take \(m=n+2\); then \(2\mid f(n+2)-f(n)\), i.e. \(f(n+2)\equiv f(n)\pmod 2\).
Letting \(m=n+k\) for \(k\ge 1\), the condition gives \(k\mid f(n+k)-f(n)\), i.e. \(\;f(n+k)\equiv f(n)\pmod{k}\).

\[
f(n)\equiv f(1)\pmod{n-1}\quad (n\ge2).
\]
Taking \(n=p+1\) where \(p\) is prime gives
\[
f(p+1)\equiv f(1)\pmod p,
\]
and combining this with the original condition for \((m,n)=(p+1,1)\) forces
\[
f(p+1)=f(1)\ \text{for every prime }p.
Take \(n=2\) and let \(m=p+2\) with \(p\) prime; then \((m-n)=p\) divides \(f(p+2)-f(2)\), so
\[

Let \(m=p+2,\ n=1\) with \(p\) prime; then \(p+1\mid f(p+2)-f(1)\), so \(f(p+2)\equiv f(1)\pmod{p+1}\).
Take \(m=p+2,\ n=2\) for prime \(p\): then \(p \mid f(p+2)-f(2)\), i.e. \(\boxed{\,f(p+2)\equiv f(2)\pmod p\,}\).

Since opposite entries must sum to a constant \(S\), we must have a circle with an even number of positions, so \(100\) positions form \(50\) opposite pairs \((a_i,\, S-a_i)\).
Let \(S=101\); then each opposite pair must be \((1,100),(2,99),\dots,(50,51)\), so we just need to pair these \(50\) complementary numbers into the \(50\) opposite slots (order within each pair and the pairing of pairs are forced).
\[
\text{Each opposite pair can be oriented in }2\text{ ways, so with }50\text{ pairs the total is }2^{50}.
\]
Since opposite pairs occupy distinct opposite-slot positions around the circle, the number of distinct (up to rotation) arrangements is \(\frac{2^{50}}{100/2}=\frac{2^{50}}{50}\), so the answer is \(\boxed{\frac{2^{50}}{50}}\).

Let \(T(x,y,z)=(x,y,z)\) and define “\(S\) covers all special triples” as: for every \((a,b,c)\) with \(a+b+c=1\), there exists \((x,y,z)\in S\) such that at least two coordinates satisfy \(x>a,\ y>b,\ z>c\); equivalently, for each \((a,b,c)\) there is \((x,y,z)\in S\) with at most one of \(x\le a,\ y\le b,\ z\le c\) holding.
Observe that this is equivalent to requiring that for every special \((a,b,c)\), the set \(S\) contains a triple \((x,y,z)\) lying strictly “above” \((a,b,c)\) in at least two coordinates, i.e. such that
\[
(x>a\ \&\ y>b)\ \text{or}\ (x>a\ \&\ z>c)\ \text{or}\ (y>b\ \&\ z>c).
\]
Let \(S=\{(x_i,y_i,z_i)\}_{i=1}^n\); then the covering condition is
\[
\forall(a,b,c)\ (a+b+c=1),\ \exists i:\ \bigl(x_i>a,\ y_i>b\bigr)\ \vee\ \bigl(x_i>a,\ z_i>c\bigr)\ \vee\ \bigl(y_i>b,\ z_i>c\bigr),
\]
equivalently, \(\forall(a,b,c)\) there is \(i\) such that at most one of the inequalities \(x_i\le a,\ y_i\le b,\ z_i\le c\) holds.
Fix \(i\) and set \(x=x_i,\ y=y_i,\ z=z_i\).  The condition “\((x,y,z)\) is **not** better than \((a,b,c)\)” means that at least two of the comparisons fail, i.e. at least two of \(x\le a,\ y\le b,\ z\le c\) hold; since \(a+b+c=1\) and \(x+y+z=1\), this is equivalent to
\[
(a,b,c)\ \in\ R_i:=\{(a,b,c)\ge 0:\ a\ge x,\ b\ge y\}\ \cup\ \{a\ge x,\ c\ge z\}\ \cup\ \{b\ge y,\ c\ge z\}.
\]
Thus \(S\) covers all special triples iff
\[
\Delta:=\{(a,b,c)\ge 0:\ a+b+c=1\}\ \subseteq\ \bigcup_{i=1}^n R_i.
\]
Therefore, to make the union cover the whole simplex \(\Delta\), it suffices to characterize how many of the regions \(R_i\) are needed to cover the set of points where at least two of the inequalities \(a\ge x_i,\ b\ge y_i,\ c\ge z_i\) hold; in particular, along any edge of \(\Delta\) (say \(c=0\)), the condition reduces to covering the interval \(\{(a,b,0):a+b=1,\ a,b\ge0\}\) by the projections of those \(R_i\) for which two coordinates can simultaneously satisfy the required comparisons.
Consider the edge \(c=0\), i.e. points \((a,1-a,0)\) with \(a\in[0,1]\). For a fixed \((x_i,y_i,z_i)\), since \(c=0\le z_i\) unless \(z_i=0\), the condition “at most one of \(x_i\le a,\ y_i\le 1-a,\ z_i\le 0\) holds” can only be violated (so coverage can fail) if the triple satisfies two coordinate inequalities among
\[
x_i\le a,\qquad y_i\le 1-a,\qquad z_i=0.
\]
Hence, along this edge, every triple with \(z_i>0\) can cover at most the region where \(x_i>a\) or \(y_i>1-a\), so failure forces \(x_i\le a\) and \(y_i\le 1-a\) simultaneously, i.e. \(a\in[x_i,\,1-y_i]\) (which is nonempty iff \(x_i+y_i\le 1\)). Therefore, to ensure coverage of the whole edge, we must have
\[
[0,1]\ \subseteq\ \bigcup_{i:\,x_i+y_i\ge 1}\bigl([0,x_i)\ \cup\ (1-y_i,1]\bigr),
\]
equivalently the uncovered set \(\{a: x_i\le a\le 1-y_i \text{ for all } i \text{ with } x_i+y_i<1\}\) is empty.
Along the edge \(c=0\), the coverage condition becomes
\[
[0,1]\subseteq \bigcup_{i:\,x_i+y_i\ge 1}\bigl([0,x_i)\ \cup\ (1-y_i,1]\bigr),
\]
so we must have
\[
\bigcap_{i:\,x_i+y_i<1}[\,x_i,\ 1-y_i\,]=\varnothing
\quad\text{(equivalently, no }a\in[0,1]\text{ satisfies }x_i\le a\le 1-y_i\ \forall i\text{ with }x_i+y_i<1).
\]
Let \(A_i:=[x_i,\,1-y_i]\) for those \(i\) with \(x_i+y_i<1\); then the edge \(c=0\) is covered iff \(\bigcap_{x_i+y_i<1} A_i=\varnothing\), i.e.
\[
\max_{x_i+y_i<1} x_i \;>\; \min_{x_i+y_i<1}(1-y_i),
\]
equivalently
\[
\max_{x_i+y_i<1} x_i \;+\;\max_{x_i+y_i<1} y_i \;>\; 1.
\]
Let
\[
m_x=\max_{\,i:\,x_i+y_i<1} x_i,\qquad m_y=\max_{\,i:\,x_i+y_i<1} y_i,
\]
then the edge \(c=0\) is covered iff \(m_x+m_y>1\).

Therefore, to make the union cover the whole simplex \(\Delta\), it suffices to characterize how many of the regions \(R_i\) are needed to cover the set of points where at least two of the inequalities \(a\ge x_i,\ b\ge y_i,\ c\ge z_i\) hold; in particular, along any edge of \(\Delta\) (say \(c=0\)), the condition reduces to covering the interval \(\{(a,b,0):a+b=1,\ a,b\ge0\}\) by the projections of those \(R_i\) for which two coordinates can simultaneously satisfy the required comparisons.

Consider the edge \(c=0\), i.e. points \((a,1-a,0)\) with \(a\in[0,1]\). For a fixed \((x_i,y_i,z_i)\), since \(c=0\le z_i\) unless \(z_i=0\), the condition “at most one of \(x_i\le a,\ y_i\le 1-a,\ z_i\le 0\) holds” can only be violated (so coverage can fail) if the triple satisfies two coordinate inequalities among
\[
x_i\le a,\qquad y_i\le 1-a,\qquad z_i=0.
\]
Hence, along this edge, every triple with \(z_i>0\) can cover at most the region where \(x_i>a\) or \(y_i>1-a\), so failure forces \(x_i\le a\) and \(y_i\le 1-a\) simultaneously, i.e. \(a\in[x_i,\,1-y_i]\) (which is nonempty iff \(x_i+y_i\le 1\)). Therefore, to ensure coverage of the whole edge, we must have
\[
[0,1]\ \subseteq\ \bigcup_{i:\,x_i+y_i\ge 1}\bigl([0,x_i)\ \cup\ (1-y_i,1]\bigr),
\]
equivalently the uncovered set \(\{a: x_i\le a\le 1-y_i \text{ for all } i \text{ with } x_i+y_i<1\}\) is empty.

Along the edge \(c=0\), the coverage condition becomes
\[
[0,1]\subseteq \bigcup_{i:\,x_i+y_i\ge 1}\bigl([0,x_i)\ \cup\ (1-y_i,1]\bigr),
\]
so we must have
\[
\bigcap_{i:\,x_i+y_i<1}[\,x_i,\ 1-y_i\,]=\varnothing
\quad\text{(equivalently, no }a\in[0,1]\text{ satisfies }x_i\le a\le 1-y_i\ \forall i\text{ with }x_i+y_i<1).
\]

Let \(A_i:=[x_i,\,1-y_i]\) for those \(i\) with \(x_i+y_i<1\); then the edge \(c=0\) is covered iff \(\bigcap_{x_i+y_i<1} A_i=\varnothing\), i.e.
\[
\max_{x_i+y_i<1} x_i \;>\; \min_{x_i+y_i<1}(1-y_i),
\]
equivalently
\[
\max_{x_i+y_i<1} x_i \;+\;\max_{x_i+y_i<1} y_i \;>\; 1.
\]

Let
\[
m_x=\max_{\,i:\,x_i+y_i<1} x_i,\qquad m_y=\max_{\,i:\,x_i+y_i<1} y_i,
\]
then the edge \(c=0\) is covered iff \(m_x+m_y>1\).

Let \(P=(x,y)\) and identify \((u,v)=f(x,y)\) with the complex number \(u+iv\); then
\[
(x^{2}-y^{2})+i(2xy-y^{2})=(x+iy)^{2}-i\,y^{2},
\]
so instead use polar form \(z=x+iy=re^{i\theta}\) to compute \(|f(P)|\) from the given coordinates.
Let \(z=x+iy=\rho e^{i\theta}\) with \(\rho=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\); then
\[
f(P)=\big(x^{2}-y^{2},\,2xy-y^{2}\big)\quad\Rightarrow\quad |f(P)|^{2}=(x^{2}-y^{2})^{2}+(2xy-y^{2})^{2}
= x^{4}+y^{4}+2x^{2}y^{2}-4y^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})+4x^{2}y^{2}
= \rho^{4}\!\left(1-4\sin^{2}\theta+4\sin^{4}\theta\right)
= \rho^{4}\bigl(2\sin^{2}\theta-1\bigr)^{2}.
\]
Thus \(|f(P)|=\rho^{2}\,|2\sin^{2}\theta-1|=\rho^{2}\,|\cos 2\theta|\), so for the iteration to approach \((0,0)\) it is necessary and sufficient that \(\rho^{2}|\cos 2\theta|<1\).
For convergence we need \(\rho^{2}|\cos 2\theta|<1\), so the set \(S\) is exactly \(\{(\rho,\theta):0\le\rho<\sqrt{1/|\cos 2\theta|}\}\) (excluding angles with \(\cos 2\theta=0\), which have no points), hence its area is
\[
\text{Area}(S)=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{1/|\cos 2\theta|}}\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta
=\frac12\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{|\cos 2\theta|}\,d\theta. 
\]
\[
\text{Area}(S)=\frac12\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{|\cos 2\theta|}\,d\theta
=\frac12\cdot 4\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\sec(2\theta)\,d\theta
=2\left[\frac12\ln|\sec(2\theta)+\tan(2\theta)|\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}
=\ln\bigl(\sec(\pi/2)+\tan(\pi/2)\bigr)\Big|_{0}^{\pi/4}.
\]
\[
\text{Area}(S)=2\left[\frac12\ln\left(\sec(2\theta)+\tan(2\theta)\right)\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}
=\left[\ln\left(\sec(2\theta)+\tan(2\theta)\right)\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}
=\ln\left(\lim_{\theta\to(\pi/4)^-}\left(\sec(2\theta)+\tan(2\theta)\right)\right)-\ln(\sec 0+\tan 0).
\]
\[
\text{Area}(S)=\lim_{\theta\to(\pi/4)^-}\ln\!\left(\sec(2\theta)+\tan(2\theta)\right)-\ln(1)
=\lim_{\theta\to(\pi/4)^-}\ln\!\left(\frac{1+\sin(2\theta)}{\cos(2\theta)}\right)
\sim \lim_{\theta\to(\pi/4)^-}\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{\cos(2\theta)}\right)
=\ln 2-\ln\!\bigl(\cos(2\theta)\bigr)\to\infty.
\]
\[
\text{Since }|\cos 2\theta|=0\text{ on a set of angles of positive measure, the condition }\rho^{2}|\cos 2\theta|<1\text{ forces the radial bound to be unbounded as }|\cos 2\theta|\to0,\text{ so }\text{Area}(S)=\frac12\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{|\cos 2\theta|}\,d\theta\text{ diverges to }\infty.
\]
Thus \(\text{Area}(S)=\infty\), so the expression \(\pi\sqrt{r}\) with \(r>0\) is impossible; therefore no finite \(r\) satisfies the problem statement.

Let the greedy partial sums be \(s_i=x_1+\cdots+x_i\) (with \(s_0=0\)); then at step \(i\) George chooses \(x_i\) to make \(|s_i|\) as small as possible among the remaining choices.
Let \(t_{i-1}=|s_{i-1}|\). George can always pick the remaining number \(a\) with \(\operatorname{sign}(a)=-\operatorname{sign}(s_{i-1})\) so that the new partial sum satisfies
\[
|s_i|=\bigl||s_{i-1}|-|a|\bigr|\le \frac12\,|s_{i-1}|,
\]
because among the remaining numbers there must exist one with absolute value at least \(t_{i-1}\) (otherwise all remaining have \(|a|<t_{i-1}\), in which case any completion would keep every partial sum within \([-(t_{i-1}),t_{i-1}]\), contradicting the optimality bound \(D\)); hence inductively the greedy walk obeys \(|s_i|\le 2D\) for all \(i\), i.e. \(G\le 2D\).

If we place 31 nonattacking knights on an \(8\times 8\) board, the complement set has \(64-31=33\) empty squares, so the number of valid placements equals the number of independent sets of size \(31\) in the knight-move graph (equivalently, independent sets of size \(33\) in the complement), which is computed by counting all independent sets via the board’s knight adjacency structure.
\[
\text{No two knights can attack }\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\text{the occupied squares form an independent set of size }31\text{ in the knight graph }G.

\]

Since \(r_1,r_2\in\mathbb{Q}\) are distinct and \(r_1r_2=-\frac{p_3}{p_1}\), we have
\[
r_1r_2=\left(\frac{a}{p_1}\right)\left(\frac{b}{p_1}\right)=\frac{ab}{p_1^2}=-\frac{p_3}{p_1}\ \Rightarrow\ ab=-p_1p_3,
\]
so \(a,b\) are nonzero integers with \(a\mid p_1p_3\) and \(b=-\frac{p_1p_3}{a}\), giving distinct rational roots \(\frac{a}{p_1}\neq -\frac{p_1p_3}{a p_1}\).

Let \(P\) be any point in \(\mathbb R^2\) and let \(u\) be any unit vector; then the square with vertices \(P,\;P+u,\;P+u+v,\;P+v\) (where \(v\) is \(u\) rotated by \(90^\circ\)) gives
\[
f(P)+f(P+u)+f(P+u+v)+f(P+v)=0. \]
Let \(u\) be replaced by \(-u\) in the same square (so the vertices are \(P,\;P-u,\;P-u+v,\;P+v\) with \(v\) still a \(90^\circ\) rotation of \(-u\)), giving
\[
f(P)+f(P-u)+f(P-u+v)+f(P+v)=0. \]
Subtracting the two obtained equations gives  
\[
\bigl(f(P+u)+f(P+u+v)\bigr)-\bigl(f(P-u)+f(P-u+v)\bigr)=0,
\]
so
\[
f(P+u)+f(P+u+v)=f(P-u)+f(P-u+v). \]
Fix \(P\) and a unit vector \(u\), and let \(v\) be \(u\) rotated by \(90^\circ\); then applying the relation also with the unit vector \(u+v\) (and the corresponding perpendicular rotation) yields that the sum \(f(x)+f(x+v)\) is constant along translates by \(u\), hence \(f(x)+f(x+v)\) is independent of \(x\), i.e. there exists a constant \(c\) (depending only on the direction \(v\)) such that \(f(x)+f(x+v)=c\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R^2\).
Let \(v\) be any unit vector and \(c(v)\) the constant such that \(f(x)+f(x+v)=c(v)\) for all \(x\); applying this to \(x-v\) gives \(f(x-v)+f(x)=c(v)\), so subtracting from \(f(x)+f(x+v)=c(v)\) yields
\[
f(x+v)-f(x-v)=c(v)-c(v)=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad f(x+v)=f(x-v)\ \text{ for all }x.
\]
Let \(v\) be any unit vector and \(t\in\mathbb R\). By applying \(f(x+v)=f(x-v)\) repeatedly along the line through \(x\) in direction \(v\), we get \(f(x+tv)=f(x)\) for all \(x\) and all \(t\); hence \(f\) is constant on every line parallel to \(v\). Since this holds for every direction \(v\), \(f\) must be constant on \(\mathbb R^2\), i.e. \(f(x)\equiv k\).
Substituting \(f(x)\equiv k\) into \(f(A)+f(B)+f(C)+f(D)=0\) for any unit square gives \(4k=0\), so \(k=0\). Hence \(f(x,y)\equiv 0\) for all \((x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\). \(\boxed{f\equiv 0}\)

Since a corner square has exactly 2 orthogonal neighbors, to satisfy “adjacent to at least two others of its own colour,” both of those neighbors must be the same colour as the corner.
Thus every corner’s two orthogonal neighbors must share its colour, so the two edge squares adjacent to that corner must have the same colour as that corner.
Consider an edge square \(e\) not at a corner: it has exactly 3 orthogonal neighbors (2 along the edge and 1 inward), and it must have at least two of them in its own colour; but along the edge, the two corner-adjacent squares already have fixed colours, so the two edge-neighbors of \(e\) must both match \(e\)’s colour, forcing the entire length-4 edge segment to be monochromatic.
Therefore the two edge-neighbors of any non-corner edge square must equal its colour, and since the corner-adjacent edge squares are already forced to match the corner, the whole boundary of the board is forced to be monochromatic.
Since all boundary squares are forced to have the same colour, any interior square adjacent orthogonally to the boundary has at least one neighbor of that boundary colour, and to have **at least two** orthogonal neighbors of its own colour it must itself match that colour; hence all interior squares also become forced to the same colour. Therefore the board can use at most **1** colour.
\[
\text{Since the constraints force every square to have the same colour, the maximum number of colours is } \boxed{1}.
\]

\]
\[
\text{Therefore Janice’s current age is } \boxed{4}.
\]

Since among the \(3\) mathematicians that must form a triangle, each edge uses two acquaintances, the smallest \(k\) forcing a triangle in any \(n\)-vertex \(k\)-regular acquaintance graph is the one guaranteed by Mantel’s theorem, giving \(k_{\min}=\left\lfloor \frac{2(n-1)}{3}\right\rfloor\).
So the required smallest guaranteed value is \(\displaystyle k_{\min}=\left\lfloor \frac{2(n-1)}{3}\right\rfloor\).
By Mantel’s theorem, the maximum number of edges in a triangle-free graph on \(n\) vertices is \(\left\lfloor \frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor\), so if the \(k\)-regular graph has \(e=\frac{nk}{2}>\left\lfloor \frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor\), a triangle must exist, hence \(k>\frac{n}{2}\); therefore the smallest such guaranteed \(k\) is \(\boxed{\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1}\).

Let \(z=x+iy\) with \(x>0,\ y>0\); then \(\bar z=x-iy\) and
\[
z^{n}=(\bar z)^{n}\iff \left(\frac{z}{\bar z}\right)^{n}=1.
\]
Let \(z=x+iy\) with \(x,y>0\). Then \(\dfrac{z}{\bar z}=\dfrac{x+iy}{x-iy}\) has modulus \(1\), so it equals \(e^{i\theta}\) where \(\theta=2\arg(z)\); hence \( \left(\dfrac{z}{\bar z}\right)^n=1 \iff e^{in\theta}=1 \iff n\theta\in 2\pi\mathbb Z\), i.e. \(\arg(z)=\frac{k\pi}{n}\) for some integer \(k\).
Since \(x,y>0\), we have \(\arg(z)=\theta\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2})\), so we need \(\frac{k\pi}{n}\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2})\), which is achieved first when \(\frac{k}{n}=\frac{1}{4}\) (take \(k=1\)), giving \(n=4\).
Take \(k=1\) so \(\arg(z)=\frac{\pi}{4}\), hence the smallest \(n\) is \(\boxed{4}\).

\[

\]

For each team \(i\), the number of opponents it actually plays is \(\mathrm{Binomial}(5,\tfrac12)\), so
\[
\Pr(\text{team }i\text{ goes undefeated}\mid k)=\left(\tfrac12\right)^k
\]
where \(k\) is that binomial random variable.
Let \(X\) be the number of undefeated teams; by linearity of expectation,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=1}^6 \Pr(\text{team }i\text{ is undefeated})=6\cdot \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\tfrac12\right)^{K}\right],
\quad K\sim \mathrm{Binomial}(5,\tfrac12). 
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\tfrac12\right)^K\right]=\sum_{k=0}^{5}\left(\tfrac12\right)^k \binom{5}{k}\left(\tfrac12\right)^k\left(\tfrac12\right)^{5-k}
=\sum_{k=0}^{5}\binom{5}{k}\left(\tfrac12\right)^{5+k}
=\left(\tfrac12\right)^5\left(1+\tfrac12\right)^5=\left(\tfrac34\right)^5.
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=6\left(\tfrac34\right)^5. \boxed{\;6\left(\tfrac34\right)^5\;}
\]

\]

\[

\]
so in particular \(v_2(20^x+14^{2y})=2m+v_2\!\left(5^{m}2^{2(x-m)}+7^{2m}2^{2(y-m)}\right)\).
WLOG assume \(x\le y\) (otherwise swap the roles of \(x\) and \(y\)); then \(m=x\) and

\]

Since any monochromatic axis-parallel rectangle would require two equal-colored dots in one row and the same two columns to also be monochromatic in another row, we must enforce that for every pair of rows, the set of column positions colored red in one row cannot equal the same set of column positions colored red in the other row (otherwise those two rows would form a monochromatic rectangle).
There are \(\binom{4}{0}+\binom{4}{1}+\binom{4}{2}+\binom{4}{3}+\binom{4}{4}=2^4\) possible red-column-sets for each row, and we must choose \(3\) distinct such sets (one for each row), so the number of valid colorings is \(P(2^4,3)=2^4(2^4-1)(2^4-2)=16\cdot 15\cdot 14=\boxed{3360}\).

Let \(P\) be the set of primes in \(\{1,\dots,100\}\) and \(M\) the set of multiples of \(4\); then \(|P|=25,\ |M|=25,\) so for any subset \(S\), letting \(p(S)\) be the number of primes and \(m(S)\) the number of multiples of 4, the condition is \(p(S)>m(S)\).

\[
N=\frac12\left(2^{50}-\binom{50}{25}\right)=2^{49}-\frac12\binom{50}{25}.
\]
Compute \(\binom{50}{25}\) modulo \(2\) using \(v_2\!\left(\binom{2n}{n}\right)=s_2(n)\) for \(n=25\): since \(25=11001_2\), \(s_2(25)=3\), so \(v_2\!\left(\binom{50}{25}\right)=3\) and hence \(\binom{50}{25}=8\cdot(\text{odd})\), giving
\[
N=2^{49}-\frac12\binom{50}{25}=2^{49}-4\cdot(\text{odd})=2^4\bigl(2^{45}-(\text{odd})\bigr),
\]
so \(v_2(N)=4\).
\[
v_2(N)=4\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the largest integer }k\text{ with }2^k\mid N\text{ is }k=4,\ \boxed{4}.
\]

\[

\]

Let the peacock be \(N=10a+b\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are the first and last 5 digits (each with no repeated digits and disjoint digit sets), so the condition “exactly twice another peacock” means \(N=2M\) for some 10-digit \(M\) with the same digit-usage property.
Since \(N=10a+b\) and \(N=2M\) with \(M\) also a 10-digit integer, the last digit satisfies \(b=2\cdot(\text{last digit of }M)\), so \(b\in\{2,4,6,8,0\}\) and in particular \(b\) must be even and \(N\equiv 2b \pmod{20}\).
Since \(N\) uses each digit once, \(N\) is not divisible by \(5\), so \(b\neq 0\); thus \(b\in\{2,4,6,8\}\) and therefore \(N\equiv 2b\in\{4,8,12,16\}\pmod{20}\).

For \(x\in(0,1]\), define \(F_n(x)=\int_0^x f_n(t)\,dt\); then \(F_n'(x)=f_n(x)\) and
\[
f_{n+1}(x)=\frac{1}{x}F_n(x)\quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{n+1}(x)=\int_0^x f_{n+1}(u)\,du=\int_0^x \frac{F_n(u)}{u}\,du. 
\]
Let \(x\in(0,1]\) and set \(H_n(x)=F_n(x)/x^{\,n}\); then
\[
F_{n+1}(x)=\int_0^x \frac{F_n(u)}{u}\,du
=\int_0^x \frac{u^{n}H_n(u)}{u}\,du
=\int_0^x u^{n-1}H_n(u)\,du,
\]
so differentiating \(H_{n+1}(x)=F_{n+1}(x)/x^{n+1}\) gives
\[
H_{n+1}(x)=\frac{1}{x^{n+1}}\int_0^x u^{n-1}H_n(u)\,du. 
\]
Differentiate \(x^{n+1}H_{n+1}(x)=\int_{0}^{x}u^{n-1}H_n(u)\,du\) to get
\[
(n+1)x^{n}H_{n+1}(x)+x^{n+1}H_{n+1}'(x)=x^{n-1}H_n(x).\]
\[
x\,H_{n+1}'(x)+(n+1)H_{n+1}(x)=\frac{H_n(x)}{x^{n-1}}=x\,\frac{F_n(x)}{x^{n}}=x\,H_n(x).
\]
Solve the linear differential recurrence
\[
H_{n+1}'(x)+\frac{n+1}{x}H_{n+1}(x)=H_n(x)
\]
by using the integrating factor \(x^{n+1}\), yielding
\[
\bigl(x^{n+1}H_{n+1}(x)\bigr)'=x^{n}H_n(x).\]
Integrating from \(0\) to \(x\) gives
\[
x^{n+1}H_{n+1}(x)-\underbrace{\lim_{t\to 0^+} t^{n+1}H_{n+1}(t)}_{=0}=\int_0^x u^{n}H_n(u)\,du,
\]
so
\[
x^{n+1}H_{n+1}(x)=\int_0^x u^{n}H_n(u)\,du. \]
\[
x^{n+1}H_{n+1}(x)=\int_{0}^{x}u^{n}H_n(u)\,du
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
H_n(x)=\frac{1}{(n-1)!}\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)^{\,n-1}g(xs)\,ds
\ \ \text{(by iterating the identity).}
\]
\[
\text{Hence }f_n(x)=F_n'(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\Bigl(x^n H_n(x)\Bigr)\sim \frac{1}{(n-1)!}\int_0^1(1-s)^{n-1}g'(xs)\,s\,ds\ \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\ g(x),
\]
so \(\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x)=\boxed{g(x)}\).

Let \(x\neq 0\) with \(|x|=1\) (so \(x^{n-2}=\frac{x^{n}}{x^{2}}\) and \(x^{n}=\overline{x}\) on \(|x|=1\)), then from
\[
x^n-x^{n-2}-x+2=0
\]
multiply by \(x^2\) to get
\[
x^{n+2}-x^n-x^3+2x^2=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad x^{n+2}-x^n = x^3-2x^2
\]
and hence \(\,x^n(x^2-1)=x^2(x-2)\,\).
Since \(|x|=1\), we have \(x\neq 0\) and thus
\[
x^n(x^2-1)=x^2(x-2)\ \Longrightarrow\ x^2-1=x^2\frac{x-2}{x^n},
\]
so taking absolute values gives
\[
|x^2-1|=|x|^2\left|\frac{x-2}{x^n}\right|=|x-2|.
\]
Square both sides: \(|x^2-1|^2=|x-2|^2\), i.e. \((x^2-1)(\overline{x}^2-1)=(x-2)(\overline{x}-2)\), with \(\overline{x}=1/x\) since \(|x|=1\).
\[
(x^2-1)\left(\frac1{x^2}-1\right)=(x-2)\left(\frac1x-2\right)\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{(x^2-1)^2}{x^2}=\frac{(x-2)^2}{x}\ \Longrightarrow\ (x^2-1)^2=x(x-2)^2.
\]
Let \(|x|=1\) so \(\overline{x}=1/x\); then from \((x^2-1)^2=x(x-2)^2\) expand and simplify:
\[
(x^4-2x^2+1)=x(x^2-4x+4)=x^3-4x^2+4x
\]
so
\[
x^4-x^3+2x^2-4x+1=0.
\]
Factor the obtained quartic:
\[
x^4-x^3+2x^2-4x+1=(x^2+ax-1)(x^2+bx-1)
\]
so comparing coefficients gives \(a+b=-1,\ ab+(-2) =2,\ -a-b=-4\), hence \(a=2,\ b=-3\), and therefore
\[
x^4-x^3+2x^2-4x+1=(x^2+2x-1)(x^2-3x-1).
\]
\[
|x|=1 \ \text{and}\ x^2+2x-1=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=\,-1\pm\sqrt2\ \text{(both real)}\ \Rightarrow\ |x|\neq 1 \ \text{so no solutions from }x^2+2x-1=0.
\]
Thus we must have \(x^2-3x-1=0\), so \(x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{13}}{2}\) and consequently \(|x|\neq 1\) (both roots are real with absolute values \(>1\)), hence there is **no** complex number \(x\) on the unit circle satisfying the original equation for any \(n\ge2\).
Since for \(|x|=1\) any solution must satisfy \((x^2+2x-1)(x^2-3x-1)=0\) and both quadratic factors have roots with \(|x|\ne 1\), there are **no** complex numbers \(x\) with \(|x|=1\) satisfying \(x^n-x^{n-2}-x+2=0\) for any \(n\ge2\). Hence the set of such \(x\) is \(\boxed{\varnothing}\).
